items.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a fast, efficient AI model for coding and agentic workflows, available across Google AI Studio and paid tiers [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen
items.summary:
Google DeepMind introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a new AI model designed for rapid execution in diverse coding and agentic workflows. It complements the more complex Gemini 4 Carbon and Argon models by focusing on speed and efficiency, and is integrated into Google AI Studio, Gemini API, Google Search, and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscriptions.

Hydrogen outperforms previous models in speed and accuracy, completing tasks 2.5 times faster than its predecessor and significantly reducing errors. It supports large context windows with a flat pricing model and excels in multi-model workflows through Google Antigravity's Orchestrator, which dynamically switches between models to optimize performance and cost. The model is effective in software development, debugging, multimodal knowledge work, and web development, offering improved productivity for developers and enterprises.

items.title: Edge0 releases Edge0-145B, the first open-source 145-billion-parameter AI model designed for on-device use with unified inference and deployment tools [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer
items.summary:
Edge0 has open-sourced Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B, AI models with up to 145 billion parameters that run locally on personal computers, offering coding, reasoning, and agent capabilities comparable to leading cloud models. The release includes the full software stack, enabling developers to reproduce results, fine-tune models, and integrate them into applications without relying on cloud services.

The models overcome traditional hardware limitations by sharing large matrices across sparse experts, optimizing training for local execution, and using a multi-tiered memory and processing approach that balances GPU, CPU, and SSD resources. Edge0-145B achieves over 80 tokens per second on laptops with 28GB peak memory, significantly advancing on-device AI performance beyond previous smaller models constrained by memory and power.

items.title: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator in Antigravity, combining models for efficient, high-quality coding and agentic workflows [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator
items.summary:
Google has introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen and a new model option called Orchestrator within its Antigravity platform, pairing Hydrogen with stronger models like Gemini 4 Carbon to optimize quality, efficiency, and latency for complex tasks. Orchestrator dynamically switches between models during task execution to improve speed and reduce resource use, achieving near-Carbon success rates while consuming 24% less quota and completing tasks 19% faster on Terminal-Bench 4.1.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen is also available as a standalone model for everyday coding, scoring highly on industry benchmarks. The Antigravity SDK allows developers to programmatically combine Hydrogen and Carbon agents for workflows such as automated open-source issue triage and code generation. These features are rolling out to paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, with enterprise access planned through Gemini for Business.

items.title: Apple launches Foundation Models framework with Swift API for integrating large language models, supporting on-device and cloud models including Claude and Gemini [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Foundation Models framework
items.summary:
Apple has introduced the Foundation Models framework, a native Swift API designed to integrate large language models into apps with features like guided generation, tool calling, image understanding, and Dynamic Profiles. The framework supports Apple’s on-device models as well as third-party server models such as Claude and Gemini, enabling developers to build AI-powered experiences that prioritize privacy and performance.

The framework includes multimodal prompts for image and text processing, integration with the Vision framework for OCR and barcode scanning, and Private Cloud Compute access for eligible developers with no cloud API cost. Additional tools include an Evaluations framework for testing prompts, a command-line interface for scripting, and open-source utilities to extend AI capabilities across Swift and Python environments.

items.title: Researchers introduce FairSumEval, an evidence-aware framework to evaluate discharge summary generation by distinguishing evidence-supported and unsupported content [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Discharge Summary Generation Is Not Just Summarization: A Reality Check for Evaluation
items.summary:
Researchers present FairSumEval, a fact-level evaluation framework for discharge summary generation that assesses whether each fact in physician-written references and model-generated summaries is supported by prior clinical evidence. The framework uses two metrics, Soft IoU-S and Soft IoU-NS, to measure agreement on facts with and without identified evidence support, revealing differences in model performance and limitations of conventional metrics.

Applying FairSumEval to 200 MIMIC-III admissions, the study finds that only 18.8% of physician reference facts have identified support in prior clinical notes, compared with over 60% for facts generated by general-purpose and medically specialized models. The framework highlights that overlap is substantially higher for evidence-supported content than for unsupported content, and that the two agreement scores are weakly correlated, indicating that traditional evaluation methods may not fully capture the nuances of discharge summary generation.

FairSumEval provides a more nuanced understanding of what models omit or add in discharge summaries, distinguishing between evidence-grounded summarization and content without identified support, which has implications for improving evaluation and development of clinical summarization models.
items.description:
Researchers present FairSumEval, a fact-level evaluation framework for discharge summary generation that assesses whether each fact in physician-written references and model-generated summaries is supported by prior clinical evidence. The framework uses two metrics, Soft IoU-S and Soft IoU-NS, to measure agreement on facts with and without identified evidence support, revealing differences in model performance and limitations of conventional metrics.

Applying FairSumEval to 200 MIMIC-III admissions, the study finds that only 18.8% of physician reference facts have identified support in prior clinical notes, compared with over 60% for facts generated by general-purpose and medically specialized models. The framework highlights that overlap is substantially higher for evidence-supported content than for unsupported content, and that the two agreement scores are weakly correlated, indicating that traditional evaluation methods may not fully capture the nuances of discharge summary generation.

FairSumEval provides a more nuanced understanding of what models omit or add in discharge summaries, distinguishing between evidence-grounded summarization and content without identified support, which has implications for improving evaluation and development of clinical summarization models.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discharge summaries combine a retrospective account of hospitalization with discharge-time decisions. Physician-written references therefore contain both facts supported by prior clinical notes and reference-only content, potentially reflecting clinical synthesis, handoffs, or discharge planning. Reference-only evaluation can conflate failure to recover available information with failure to reproduce content absent from the model input. We introduce FairSumEval, an evidence-aware, fact-level framework that assesses whether each reference and generated fact is supported by the model's evidence and captured by the other summary. The resulting outcome map separates matches, omissions, and additions. Two complementary metrics, Soft IoU-S and Soft IoU-NS, measure reference-generation agreement for facts with and without identified evidence support. On 200 MIMIC-III admissions, 18.8% of physician reference facts have identified support in the prior evidence, compared with 65.4% and 63.5% of facts generated by a general-purpose and a medically specialized model. Overlap is substantially higher for supported content (0.255 and 0.236) than for content without identified support (0.030 and 0.026). The two scores are weakly correlated across admissions (rho = 0.22 and 0.17), and conventional metrics do not consistently capture both dimensions. FairSumEval distinguishes evidence-grounded summarization from agreement on content without identified support, revealing what models omit and add in each category.

The framework uses two metrics, Soft IoU-S and Soft IoU-NS, to measure agreement on facts with and without identified evidence support, revealing differences in model performance and limitations of conventional metrics.

Applying FairSumEval to 200 MIMIC-III admissions, the study finds that only 18.8% of physician reference facts have identified support in prior clinical notes, compared with over 60% for facts generated by general-purpose and medically specialized models. The framework highlights that overlap is substantially higher for evidence-supported content than for unsupported content, and that the two agreement scores are weakly correlated, indicating that traditional evaluation methods may not fully capture the nuances of discharge summary generation.

FairSumEval provides a more nuanced understanding of what models omit or add in discharge summaries, distinguishing between evidence-grounded summarization and content without identified support, which has implications for improving evaluation and development of clinical summarization models.

items.title: Researchers present Parallel Prompting method to speed up LLM inference for multiple questions on the same document by decoding all questions simultaneously with shared context [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Read Once, Answer Many: Parallel Prompting for Shared-Context LLM Inference
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Parallel Prompting, a technique that processes multiple independent questions about the same long document in parallel during large language model (LLM) inference. This method reads the shared document once per decoding step for all questions, using a stream-id attention mask to keep answers conditioned on their respective questions, significantly reducing memory bandwidth constraints.

Implemented in SGLang with minimal code additions, Parallel Prompting achieves 3.7 to 6 times speedup over the standard SGLang FlashInfer backend on GPUs like the A100 and RTX A6000, tested across various document lengths and question counts. The approach maintains fixed decode step shapes captured as CUDA graphs and requires no dense tensors for masking, demonstrating consistent performance improvements across multiple runs and software releases.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.15130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM workloads sometimes ask many independent questions about the same long document, as in document QA, data labeling and LLM-based evaluation. Prefix caching removes the redundant prefill shared by these queries, but each decode step still reads the document's key-value (KV) cache once per question, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and scales with the number of questions. We present Parallel Prompting, which decodes P questions as P independent streams of a single request all at once, fixing this issue. In our method, every step reads the shared document once for all P streams, and a stream-id attention mask, evaluated inside the attention kernel, keeps each answer conditioned only on the document and its own question. We implement Parallel Prompting in SGLang by adding about 80 lines to three existing files and a small engine package; the mask needs no dense tensor, and every decode step has a fixed shape that is captured as a CUDA graph. With CodeLlama-7B, 8k-16k-token documents and 64-256 questions per document, Parallel Prompting is 3.7x faster than stock SGLang with its FlashInfer backend on an A100 and 5.9-6.0x faster on an RTX A6000, on two SGLang releases, including the most recent release. Timed on identical inputs, it is faster than stock SGLang in all 144 runs (2 GPUs x 2 releases x 6 workloads x 6 input sets). Code: https://github.com/jlab-nlp/parallel-prompting

items.title: Researchers develop a teacher-free co-evolution method for a Gemma 4 12B LLM agent that improves policy adherence and consistency using deployment logs and reinforcement learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Knowledge in the Harness, Reliability in the Weights: Teacher-Free Co-Evolution of an LLM Agent
items.summary:
Researchers present a method for improving small open language models in customer-service deployments by enabling a Gemma 4 12B agent to self-improve without a stronger teacher model. The agent reads domain policies from on-demand skills, diagnoses failed conversations, writes rules that pass rigorous validation, and uses reinforcement learning to train a LoRA adapter on multi-turn conversations. This approach improves performance on retail and airline benchmarks by significant margins, surpassing a reference agent using the full policy in its system prompt and closing much of the gap to frontier models.

The system iteratively serves fresh tasks, refines rules through code checks, self-review, retests, and noise-calibrated validation, and applies reinforcement learning to enhance reliability. Ablation studies show that the rules help solve previously unsolved tasks and encode policy knowledge not internalized by reinforcement learning alone, while trained weights improve task reliability. This method demonstrates that small models can self-correct and improve policy compliance and consistency from their own deployment data without external supervision.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.15268v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small open models suit private customer-service deployments but trail frontier models in two ways: they miss what the written policy requires in a given situation, and they act inconsistently on what they know. We study whether such a model can close both gaps from its own deployment logs and their reference outcomes, without a stronger teacher model. Our starting point is a Gemma 4 12B agent that reads its domain policy from on-demand skills rather than from its system prompt. In each round, the deployed system serves a fresh batch of tasks; the base model diagnoses failed conversations and writes rules into the skills, and a rule survives only if it passes code checks, counterexample self-review, a paired retest, and a noise-calibrated validation gate. Reinforcement learning (GRPO) then trains a LoRA adapter on complete multi-turn, tool-using conversations. On the retail and airline domains of $\tau^2$-bench, without training or selecting on official tasks, the agent after two rounds improves on this starting point by 12.5 pass$^1$ points in retail and 19.5 in airline, and by 18.4 and 22.0 pass$^4$ points. It also exceeds the benchmark's reference agent, which runs the same model with the whole policy in its system prompt, by 11.8 and 8.0 pass$^1$ points and by 22.8 and 16.0 pass$^4$ points, closing most of the gap to three frontier models under the same protocol. A $2\times2$ ablation shows that the rules rescue tasks the agent never solved and carry policy knowledge that RL with the rules in context does not internalize, whereas the trained weights make solved tasks reliable.

items.title: AutoOntic automatically induces ontologies from text to improve knowledge graph construction with type hierarchies and domain/range constraints [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AutoOntic: Automatic Ontology Induction from Text for Knowledge Graph Construction
items.summary: AutoOntic is a pipeline that constructs ontologies from text by canonicalizing entity types and relations, inducing hierarchical type structures, and mining relation-level domain and range constraints to enhance knowledge graph quality. It uses corpus-derived relation-argument profiles and LLM-based parent-child checks to organize types, enabling better entity deduplication and constraint induction. Evaluations on datasets like Wikidata-TekGen and DBpedia-WebNLG show over 90% semantic alignment with reference classes, and knowledge graphs using AutoOntic ontologies achieve 88% retrieval accuracy on MINE. The tool is publicly available on GitHub.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.15467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation depends on the quality of the knowledge graph (KG) it retrieves over, yet schema-free LLM-based extraction pipelines typically produce flat graphs: deduplicated entities and relations with no type hierarchy and no domain/range constraints. We present AutoOntic, a pipeline that automatically constructs an ontology from text by canonicalizing open-vocabulary entity types and relations, inducing a hierarchy over the canonicalized types, and mining relation-level domain and range constraints. Its hierarchy induction procedure prioritizes types using corpus-derived relation-argument profiles and places them through local, LLM-adjudicated parent/child checks, allowing newly inserted types to trigger reassignment of existing parent-child links. The resulting hierarchy constrains entity deduplication and supports the induction of relation-level domain/range constraints. For intrinsic evaluation, we introduce a reference-based protocol that classifies induced ontology types as exact, broader, narrower, or unrelated to reference domain and range classes. On the Wikidata-TekGen and DBpedia-WebNLG subsets of Text2KGBench, over 90% of AutoOntic's induced endpoint types are semantically aligned with the reference classes across two LLM backbones: about half match exactly, while most remaining differences concern granularity. On MINE, knowledge graphs organized using an ontology built by AutoOntic achieve 88% retrieval accuracy. AutoOntic is available at https://github.com/screemix/AutoOntic.

items.title: Researchers define four mechanistic observation lenses for uncertainty quantification in large language models, clarifying evaluation protocols and identifying open research directions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Where Is Uncertainty Observed? A Mechanistic Understanding of Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers propose a mechanistic framework to understand where uncertainty is observed within large language models (LLMs) to improve uncertainty quantification (UQ). They identify four observation lenses—structural, representational, distributional, and semantical—that correspond to different points in the model's computation and carry varying levels of information relevant for estimating uncertainty.

The study surveys existing UQ methods through these lenses and distinguishes evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics to clarify UQ evaluation protocols. It also highlights open problems and future research directions aimed at connecting uncertainty estimation more closely to the internal computations and downstream applications of LLMs, which is critical for assessing when model responses can be trusted.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.15735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowing when a large language model's (LLM's) response can be trusted is critical for its safe use. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) can help LLMs recognize if their responses may be unreliable. Existing taxonomies organize UQ methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism. They leave unresolved the question of where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation. The answer matters because the observation point determines whether an estimator has access to enough information to recover a given target, and how well it can recover it. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, we define four mechanistic observation lenses: the structural lens observes component updates, the representational lens observes hidden states, the distributional lens observes token probabilities, and the semantical lens observes distributions over meanings. We relate these lenses through the residual stream and order them by the information they carry, which gives a principle for selecting UQ methods for different targets. We survey existing methods through the four lenses. Furthermore, we distinguish evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics to clarify different UQ evaluation protocols. Finally, we identify open problems and research directions to connect uncertainty estimation to the internal computation and downstream use of LLMs.

items.title: SO-Arena benchmark evaluates capability spectrum and decision reliability of 21 System One models across 11 domains and five capability families [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SO-Arena: Benchmarking the Capability Spectrum and Reliability of System One Models
items.summary:
Researchers introduce SO-Arena, a benchmark designed to assess both the capability range and decision reliability of System One models, which aim for fast, general-purpose decision-making without lengthy token generation. The benchmark covers 11 domains and five capability families, using evidence-grounded evaluation, domain-specific difficulty criteria, and interactive sandbox testing to provide fine-grained assessments. It also measures decision reliability through stability under option changes and recognition of missing answers when no valid option exists.

Evaluations of 21 models reveal that scaling and additional reasoning benefits vary widely across domains, and strong overall performance does not guarantee reliable decision-making; notably, the top-performing System One model ranks only seventh in reliability. These findings emphasize the importance of considering both capability spectrum and decision reliability as complementary factors to understand the strengths and limitations of System One models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.15777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: System One models promise fast, general-purpose decision-making without lengthy token generation. However, understanding their capability spectrum and decision reliability requires more than aggregate performance on current benchmarks. Existing evaluations often provide limited insight into the breadth of model capabilities and the reliability of their decisions. We introduce SO-Arena, a benchmark characterizing the capability spectrum and decision reliability of System One models across 11 domains and five capability families. For the capability spectrum, SO-Arena offers evidence-grounded evaluation through reliable sources and manual verification of reference labels against model-visible inputs; fine-grained capability assessment through domain-specific difficulty criteria; and realistic interactive evaluation, where models iteratively execute actions in sandboxes. Reasoning-intensive tasks further enable system one-two comparison. Beyond accuracy, SO-Arena assesses decision reliability through two complementary measures: decision stability under controlled option-set changes and missing-answer recognition when no valid option is available. Evaluations across 21 models reveal that the benefits of scaling and additional reasoning vary substantially across domains. More importantly, strong overall performance does not necessarily imply reliable decision-making: the best-performing System One model ranks only seventh in reliability. Together, these findings highlight the need to characterize capability spectrum and decision reliability as complementary dimensions, providing a systematic view of the strengths and limitations of System One models.

items.title: Researchers validate and test occupational role vectors in large language models to assess role representation and control over model behavior [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Roles Do System Prompts Really Assign? Validating and Steering Occupational Role Vectors in LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers introduce a framework to extract and inject occupational role vectors in large language models, aiming to capture how individuals in specific roles respond to tasks. They validate these vectors on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct models, examining their stability, separability, and domain consistency, as well as their ability to steer model responses during conversations.

The study finds that extracted role vectors are reproducible and distinct even for similar roles, and they encode role information subtly across different domains. Injecting these vectors can enhance role expression compared to unsteered models but generally matches the effect of explicit role prompts; combining vectors with prompts strengthens role expression in single responses but does not maintain it over extended interactions. The results highlight the complexity of representing and controlling occupational roles in language model activations and responses.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.15989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Applications built on large language models assign the model a role through its system prompt, intending to shape how it responds for their use case. We introduce a validation framework for extracting and injecting occupational role vectors, activation-level directions that capture how someone in a given occupational role would distinctively respond to a task or question. We validate these vectors through two complementary lenses, on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The interpretability lens asks whether each vector is a stable, separable, domain-consistent representation of its role: extracted vectors are highly reproducible across repeated runs and sampling temperatures, remain separable even for very similar roles, and agree more with themselves across in-domain and out-of-domain questions than with other roles' signal. The control lens asks whether injecting a role vector during generation makes the model express the role, and sustain it over a conversation, as well as a role prompt does. On Qwen, injecting the vector alone makes the model express the intended role substantially more often than unsteered, but at best matches a role prompt; on both models, adding the vector to the prompt strengthens the role in single answers but did not slow the role's decline over 30 turns. Together, the two lenses show why both are needed: out of domain the role is expressed only subtly, yet the activations still encode it; and a vector that is stable and separable can still barely steer the model's behavior.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.16270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural Language Inference models can be sensitive to localized lexical changes. We introduce Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning (SMIC), which constructs a single input-dependent multiscale reference and reuses it across Transformer layers. Each layer applies its own multiscale transformation to the shared reference and injects the resulting conditioning feature before the attention update. We instantiate SMIC in a token--context Transformer (TCT) and conduct from-scratch comparisons against decoder-based and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) baselines across all three ANLI rounds. TCT-SMIC attains the highest observed ten-seed mean accuracy on all three ANLI rounds. The ablations further support the contribution of SMIC. We evaluate a real-valued Llama-style plug-in and extend deletion/insertion diagnostics to pretrained ModernBERT encoder and Llama decoder models with and without SMIC. Across the evaluated perturbation protocols, TCT-SMIC exhibits comparatively low pooled-attention redistribution and smaller signed accuracy changes. We further establish a finite-sample bound on average subset-mass redistribution in terms of the mean Jensen--Shannon divergence between the restricted and renormalized attention distributions.

items.title: Researchers identify goal encoding in large language models via specific attention heads that guide sub-goal selection and future actions across tasks and languages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Goal Encoding in LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers investigated how large language models (LLMs) internally represent goals that guide their actions flexibly across different execution paths. They designed a multi-subtask coding environment to evaluate goal-seeking behavior and localized goal encoding in a sparse set of attention heads, which also decode the model's future actions in natural language. This encoding was shown to causally influence the next action and adapt when transplanted to different programming languages, sustaining throughout task execution despite the model's lack of recurrence.

The study proposes a non-recurrent goal-seeking (NRGS) mechanism where the LLM repeatedly re-reads the goal from the task specification and compares it with progress in the context to pursue remaining objectives. The researchers tested this hypothesis through targeted causal interventions, providing insights into how LLMs maintain and utilize goal representations during complex tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate whether and how LLMs encode goals: internal neural representations that precede and guide action, and that are flexible enough to be realized through many different execution paths. We construct a coding setting with multiple sub-tasks that allows us to evaluate goal-seeking behavior and the selection of sub-goals. In this setting, we localize an encoding of the next sub-goal in the outputs of a sparse set of attention heads. The same heads can be used to decode the LM's future actions in natural language (e.g., "I'm checking if a word is a palindrome"). We verify that this encoding is causal for next action and is plastic: transplanting it into a different environment, e.g., another programming language, triggers the same operation realized with a different sequence of tokens. The LM also sustains the encoding throughout the action's execution, which is puzzling because a transformer LM without recurrence cannot carry a state forward for more tokens than it has layers left. We propose that it does not need to. Under a non-recurrent goal-seeking (NRGS) account, the LM frequently re-reads the goal from the task specification, compares it with the progress visible in the growing context, and pursues what remains. We test the predictions of this account with targeted causal interventions.

items.title: Researchers find that editing an AI agent's history to correct errors can reduce performance if the external world state still reflects those errors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cleaning an Agent's History Hurts When the World Still Holds the Error
items.summary:
Researchers studied how tool-using language-model agents handle histories of their own mistakes and found that cleaning or repairing these histories does not always improve outcomes. They tested scenarios where an agent's history was corrected while the external world state still contained errors, revealing that such corrections can sometimes worsen the agent's performance compared to leaving the history unedited.

Experiments on benchmarks like AgentCE-Bench and AppWorld showed that adding truthful notes beside errors improved recovery rates, but completing actions in the history without updating the world state lowered success rates. The study highlights that the effect of history edits depends on the consistency between the agent's history and the actual world state, suggesting that making a history appear clean while the world still holds errors can be detrimental to agent performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14654v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using language-model agents accumulate histories of their own mistakes, and a system that compacts, repairs or hands off such a history decides what it says about those mistakes while their effects stay in the world. Prior work cleans the history at a fixed world, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. We ask whether the same correct content helps or hurts depending on how the history states it and what the world holds. We freeze an agent mid-task with its exact world state, edit the history or the world, and let a receiver model continue. On AgentCE-Bench, after the agent commits a wrong value, we hold the world fixed and add the correct value by two natural edits: a truthful note beside the preserved error or the agent's own completed action. The note raises recovery, the share of remaining targets the receiver gets right, from 51% under a matched neutral note to 66%. The completed action lowers it below the unedited history, from 50% to 44%, so the value's presence alone does not predict the effect. On AppWorld, after a database write, we vary whether its receipt reports success or failure and whether its effect is present. A success receipt lowers whole-task success from 45% to 28% while the effect is absent and raises it from 38% to 49% once present. The two effects differ by 27 points pooled over two receivers, a difference positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%. A history edit's effect thus depends on the world it describes, and a history made to look clean while the world still holds the error can leave an agent worse off than no edit at all.

items.title: Researchers propose executable code explanations for LLM behavior, enabling automatic verification and improved consistency across multiple inputs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Code as Explanations: Executable and Verifiable LLM Explanations
items.summary:
Researchers propose using executable code as explanations for large language model (LLM) behavior to address the limitations of free-text explanations like chain-of-thought, which are generated per instance and hard to verify on new inputs. They introduce a Consistency metric to measure how well a program reproduces LLM outputs across datasets, finding that code explanations can be significantly shorter and better aligned with model behavior in many cases.

Experiments across three open-source code-capable LLMs and eight tasks show that code explanations achieve high consistency in several settings but struggle with tasks involving complex linguistic components. Additional tests with Claude Opus 5.5 indicate that providing consistency feedback and code execution improves explanation consistency, though challenges remain for more complex tasks. The study highlights executable code as a verifiable and compact method for explaining LLMs and suggests verification feedback as a promising avenue for enhancing explanation reliability.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly make consequential decisions and solve problems alongside humans, we must understand how models arrive at their conclusions. Understanding how an LLM behaves requires observing it across multiple inputs, yet free-text explanations such as chain-of-thought (CoT) are generated per instance and cannot be easily verified on new inputs. We propose {code explanations to address the mismatch in how LLM explanations are generated versus how they are evaluated: a program explains LLM behavior across a dataset of inputs, and its execution enables automatic verification. We define Consistency metric that measures the fraction of inputs on which the program reproduces the LLM's outputs, and use it to evaluate and select candidate programs. Across three open-source code-capable LLMs and eight tasks, we find that LLMs can produce highly consistent code explanations in several settings. Code explanations are also 6$\times$ to 100$\times$ shorter than CoT, and better align with model behavior in 9 out of 24 settings. However, consistency is significantly lower on tasks with more complex linguistic components, where generated programs reproduce model outputs no more frequently than an uninformative explanation baseline, and these programs often rely on longer hard-coded patterns. In experiments with Claude Opus 5.5, providing the model with consistency feedback and code execution improves explanation consistency across tasks, but consistency remains significantly lower on more complex tasks. Our findings establish executable code as a novel, verifiable, and compact approach to explaining LLM behavior and highlight verification feedback as a promising direction for improving explanation consistency. The code for this paper is at https://github.com/rajesh-lab/code-as-explanations.

items.title: Study evaluates proof-step verification using LLM judges on open-weight models for mathematical reasoning, finding precision gains but limited coverage and distinct failure modes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Is Proof-Step Verification Worth Its Cost? Operating Requirements of Certify-or-Decline Verification for Open-Weight Mathematical Reasoning
items.summary: Researchers assessed a proof-step verification pipeline that rewrites solver answers into typed steps and uses large language model (LLM) judges to certify or decline them across datasets including GPQA, AIME-2025, and a MATH-500 subset. Certification improved answer-key-match precision significantly on GPQA and AIME but covered only a fraction of attempts; gains on near-ceiling MATH-500 were smaller and came with reduced coverage. A diagnostic analysis revealed many problems ended with invalid proof construction before reaching a judge, and external LLM acceptance rates of certified proofs were lower than answer-key matches. The study highlights challenges in proof verification accuracy and consistency, motivating separate reporting of execution failures, selected-answer precision, and independent proof validity assessments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proof-step verification rewrites a solver's answer into typed steps and uses LLM judges to certify or decline. We evaluate this pipeline on open-weight models across GPQA, AIME-2025, and a MATH-500 subset. Certification raises answer-key-match precision by 31 percentage points on the strong GPQA configuration and 46 on AIME, while answering only 35% and 21% of attempts. On near-ceiling MATH-500, gains are at most 5 points at a loss of 13-27 points of coverage. An output-token-matched self-consistency selector obtains 82.9% precision at 35% coverage, compared with the verifier's pooled 87.6% (paired difference: +4.8 points, 95% interval [-8.2, 18.5]). A diagnostic sample reveals a distinct failure mode: 52 of 88 completed problems end in invalid proof construction without ever reaching a judge. Finally, external-LLM acceptance of rendered certified chains is 61.0-67.6%, compared with 87.6% answer-key match. These audits lack human or formal-kernel ground truth. Open-weight auditor pairs show near-zero chance-corrected agreement, which measures consistency rather than accuracy against proof truth. These results motivate separate reporting of execution failures, selected-answer precision, and independently assessed proof validity. We provide per-configuration results and evaluation details in the supplement.

items.title: Researchers distill language models by retaining only the highest-probability vocabulary fraction, reducing training costs without degrading performance on reasoning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Effective Teacher Support for Reasoning Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers propose a method to distill language models by focusing on the teacher model's highest-probability vocabulary fraction, renormalizing as support decreases from 100% to 0.01%. This approach was tested on Qwen3 and Nemotron Nano model pairs, showing no performance loss on MMLU-Pro benchmarks at very low vocabulary retention levels. The method reduces training time by 38% and peak memory usage by 24% without degrading reasoning task accuracy.

The study confirms that the reliable cutoff for vocabulary retention depends on the model family, as smaller fractions caused some models to fail emitting specific reasoning tags. The approach also caches retained next-token scores from the teacher's forward pass to optimize training efficiency. These findings suggest that selective vocabulary distillation can maintain model quality while significantly lowering computational costs during training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14850v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forward-KL language-model distillation normally computes dense teacher and student scores over the full vocabulary at every supervised position, making training and stored teacher targets expensive. We instead distill from the teacher's highest-probability vocabulary fraction, renormalizing the retained mass as we sweep support from 100% to 0.01%. Our main study distills Qwen3 4B -> 1.7B. We confirm the broader support-reduction finding on larger Qwen3 8B -> 4B and Nemotron Nano 12B -> 9B pairs and under answer-only supervision. We evaluate generation primarily on MMLU-Pro and secondarily on GPQA-Diamond. Across the Qwen3 settings, retaining 0.01% of the vocabulary causes no observed MMLU-Pro degradation relative to full-vocabulary distillation, although disagreement with the complete teacher distribution increases. Nemotron Nano matches full-vocabulary MMLU-Pro at 0.1%, but smaller fractions fail to emit the closing reasoning tag, showing that the reliable cutoff depends on the model family. At 0.01% support, caching the retained next-token scores from the teacher forward pass cuts training step time by 38%, while restricting student output computation to those tokens cuts peak memory by 24%; neither causes observed MMLU-Pro degradation.

items.title: Researchers propose Likelihood-Gated Policy Optimization to eliminate importance ratio computation in LLM reinforcement learning, maintaining stability and reducing training time by 18% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Is the Importance Ratio Necessary for Stable Reinforcement Learning in LLMs?
items.summary:
Researchers propose Likelihood-Gated Policy Optimization (LGPO) as a new reinforcement learning method for large language models (LLMs) that removes the need to compute old-policy likelihoods for importance sampling ratios. LGPO enforces a soft trust region constraint via likelihood-based gating, maintaining training stability without the overhead of importance ratio calculations.

Empirical results show that removing the importance sampling correction does not harm stability, while removing the trust region mechanism can cause training collapse. LGPO achieves comparable performance to standard methods like GRPO under typical training conditions but reduces training time by about 18%. It also remains stable in fully on-policy training scenarios where GRPO fails, enabling more efficient and robust post-training reinforcement learning for LLMs across different regimes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.15404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become central to post-training large language models (LLMs). However, popular RL methods like GRPO incur non-negligible overhead by computing both old-policy and current-policy likelihoods to form importance sampling ratios. In this work, we propose Likelihood-Gated Policy Optimization (LGPO), which enforces a soft trust region constraint via likelihood-based gating, eliminating the need to compute old-policy likelihoods. Empirically, we show that removing the importance sampling correction term does not harm training stability, whereas removing the trust region mechanism can lead to collapse. Moreover, ratio-based clipping can fail in fully on-policy training: the importance ratio stays at 1, so the ratio-based trust region constraint never activates. Under standard training settings where GRPO is stable, LGPO achieves comparable training stability and peak performance while reducing training time by ~18% on average relative to a standard implementation that recomputes old-policy likelihoods. In fully on-policy training, where GRPO fails, LGPO remains stable, enabling more efficient and robust LLM RL post-training across training regimes.

items.title: Researchers release Curiosity-0826-4B, a 4.3B-parameter generative medical event model trained on Epic Cosmos for zero-shot clinical predictions across pediatric and adult populations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Curiosity-0826-4B: Generative Medical Event Sequence Modeling Across Pediatric and Adult Populations
items.summary:
Curiosity-0826-4B is an updated generative medical event foundation model that simulates patient timelines to produce zero-shot clinical predictions, trained on Epic Cosmos data. It expands on its predecessor by including a broader patient population, richer clinical event representations, and a longer context window, achieving improved laboratory value predictions and comparable or better disease event prediction performance across pediatric and adult cohorts.
The model shows AUROCs of 0.742–0.785 for new asthma diagnosis and 0.829–0.852 for asthma exacerbation in pediatric patients aged 2–17, comparable to adult cohorts, while sickle cell crisis prediction was lower in children than adults. It also enables mortality prediction across hospice, inpatient, and ambulatory adult settings with AUROCs between 0.821 and 0.942. Curiosity-0826-4B uses scaling-law analysis for compute-optimal pretraining, requiring fewer training tokens but more floating point operations than its predecessor.
By extending zero-shot prediction to pediatric patients and additional outcomes, the model broadens opportunities for clinical and operational applications without needing separate task-specific models. Further validation is needed to assess calibration, subgroup performance, timeline completion, generalization, and prospective clinical utility.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.15710v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Curiosity-0826-4B, an updated version of the generative medical event foundation model trained on Epic Cosmos that simulates patient timelines to produce zero-shot clinical predictions. Curiosity-0826-4B incorporates a broader patient population and richer clinical event representations, while generally matching or exceeding Curiosity-0226-1B, the largest model in the previous Curiosity-0226 series, on evaluated tasks supported by both models. Laboratory value prediction improved, with MAE 18--46% lower than that of Curiosity-0226-1B. We evaluated prediction of disease events across pediatric cohorts aged 2--17 years. AUROCs for new asthma diagnosis (0.742--0.785) and asthma exacerbation (0.829--0.852) were comparable to those in the adult reference cohort, while AUROCs for sickle cell crisis (0.820--0.847) were lower than in adults (0.915). Explicit representation of documented death enabled new mortality prediction tasks among adults across hospice, inpatient, and ambulatory settings (AUROC 0.821--0.942). Scaling-law analysis guided compute-optimal initial pretraining followed by continued pretraining with context extension. The resulting Curiosity-0826-4B model has more parameters (4.3B versus 1B) and a longer context window (16K versus 8K). It processes 56% fewer training tokens and requires 2.2 times the training floating point operations (FLOPs) compared with its predecessor. By extending a common zero-shot prediction strategy to pediatric patients and additional outcomes, Curiosity-0826-4B broadens opportunities to develop clinical and operational applications without training separate task-specific models. Further validation should assess local calibration, performance across patient subgroups and event frequencies, timeline completion rates, and generalization to new settings, alongside prospective evaluation of clinical and operational utility.

items.title: Researchers analyze when verifiable-reward reinforcement learning leads models to bluff or remain honest based on payoff ratios and checker acceptance rates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Honesty Is a Race: Predicting When Verifiable-Reward RL Teaches a Model to Bluff
items.summary:
This study examines how reinforcement learning models trained with verifiable rewards can either learn to be honest or to bluff, depending on the ratio of payoffs for unverifiable versus verifiable verdicts and the acceptance rate of a checker. The authors develop a theoretical framework predicting honesty as a race influenced by training dynamics and payoff thresholds, supported by experiments on propositional Datalog, code models, and math problem abstention.

The analysis shows that when the payoff ratio exceeds a certain threshold, models tend to maintain honesty, but above a ceiling, they may incorrectly label correct programs as buggy. Experiments demonstrate that adjusting training conditions and payoffs can sustain higher honesty levels, while linear probes reveal that some truthful information remains encoded even when honesty collapses. These findings provide insights into designing reinforcement learning systems that balance truthful behavior and strategic bluffing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.15779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two rewards with the same expected payoff at the start of training can end a reinforcement-learning run in opposite places, with an honest model or one that bluffs. We study rewards that pay $b$ for a verdict that a checker cannot verify ("this program is correct") and $r$ for a certificate that it accepts (an input revealing a bug). To first order, a GRPO step makes the model more honest exactly when $\tilde{p}\,r/b>1+\kappa$. Here $\tilde{p}$ is the rate at which the checker accepts the model's certificates, weighted toward the items on which the model still gives both verdicts, and $\kappa$ is the pull of the items on which the unverifiable verdict is right. Both terms move during training. A checker raises $\tilde{p}$, so near the threshold honesty is a race, which a run just below the threshold can win and a run under a lottery (random pay with the same mean) cannot. The term $\kappa$ starts large and falls as the other items settle, so a run just above the threshold first dips toward bluffing, on code nearly to zero, before climbing back. Paying the honest verdict also pulls the other items toward it, which predicts a ceiling on the payoff ratio, above which the model gives the honest verdict where it is wrong. On propositional Datalog, two code models, and abstention on grade-school math, with $p$ the model's success rate before RL, no run above $pr/b=1$ ends collapsed, and runs under the checker can survive slightly below it. At $pr/b=3$, above the ceiling, both code models call about half of correct programs buggy. On depth-3 Datalog, training generously under the checker and then cutting the payoff keeps the model at least 67% honest in three seeds, at a ratio where the same model trained from the start falls to 4-15% and is at most 47% honest after 160 steps. On depth-2 Datalog, when honesty collapses, a linear probe fit before RL still reads the truth.

items.originalTitle: Scaling public input on AI policy with pluralistic agents
items.summary: Researchers have developed pluralistic AI agents that deliberate on behalf of individuals to align AI systems with diverse human perspectives, aiming to scale public input on AI policy. In a study involving 746 participants, these agents influenced policy preferences according to their represented personas and were viewed as useful and fair compared to single AI reasoning models. The study suggests pluralistic agents could amplify human input in AI safety policy development where direct discussion is impractical, though their influence varies based on how personas instruct them.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.16028v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI is being deployed across a vast range of application domains, cultural environments, and human stakeholders. Safe and responsible AI development requires continuously accounting for diverse perspectives. We develop and test pluralistic agents, AI agent representatives that deliberate on behalf of individuals to align AI systems with diverse human perspectives. Pluralistic agents could help people contribute to many more discussions than they could directly participate in, on technical topics that would require training, and on policy choices that rely on private information that corporations and governments cannot readily share. Our experiments identify opportunities, risks, and perceptions of pluralistic agents. Agents were able to reliably shift policies in the direction of their represented persona's preferences, but the extent of each agent's influence was sensitive to the instructions from its persona, such as having more influence when instructed to be more verbose or less cooperative. This suggests that influence in AI-assisted deliberation could vary based on how participants prompt their agents and how the system is designed. In a preregistered study, 746 humans participated in the pluralistic agents process. Participants viewed pluralistic agents as useful and fair, preferring agents over the baseline of providing input to a single AI reasoning model. Most participants preferred participating themselves over either pluralistic agents or the baseline, but pluralistic agents recovered 68% of the baseline-direct gap in reported satisfaction and 82% in fairness. Because pluralistic agents can be used in many real-world contexts where direct discussion is not, they could be a promising tool to scale AI safety policy development. We encourage cautious exploration of this method, playing to its strengths as an amplifier of human input rather than a replacement.

items.title: Researchers introduce JudgeMix, a judge-guided data synthesis framework that dynamically combines expert and target model guidance to improve LLM agent training and reduce distribution mismatch [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: JudgeMix: Judge-Guided Mixed-Rollout Data Synthesis for LLM Agents
items.summary: JudgeMix addresses the training-inference distribution mismatch in supervised fine-tuning of large language model (LLM) agents by selectively querying expert guidance only when the target model struggles, based on step-wise semantic evaluations. This approach preserves the model's correct behaviors while correcting errors, leading to higher trajectory success rates and better alignment with the target model's state distribution. Evaluated on two agentic tool-use benchmarks, AppWorld and AutomationBench, JudgeMix outperforms existing methods with improvements up to 10 pass@1 points.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.16174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories is a standard paradigm for training LLM agents. However, it suffers from a well-known training-inference distribution mismatch, calling for target-aware data synthesis strategies that ground the training data in the target model's native state distribution. To bridge this gap, emerging approaches incorporate the expert either to guide mixed rollouts alongside the target model, or to provide dense step-wise supervision. Nonetheless, existing methods apply expert assistance blind to the target model's inherent behavior: they either disrupt the rollout using sub-optimal random intervention heuristics, or they enforce indiscriminate uniform supervision that unnecessarily overwrites the model's already-correct actions. We introduce JudgeMix, a judge-guided data synthesis framework that dynamically interleaves the target model and expert based on step-wise semantic evaluations. JudgeMix queries expert guidance precisely when the target model struggles, ensuring high trajectory success rates while keeping the state distribution aligned with the target model. It additionally uses the judge evaluation to reweight expert supervision on different steps, preserving model's inherent valid behavior while correcting its errors. On two agentic tool-use benchmarks, AppWorld and AutomationBench, JudgeMix demonstrates consistent superior performance to existing methods, with improvements up to 10 pass@1 points.

items.summary:
Researchers propose Recursive State-Augmented Language Models (Recursive SALM), a framework that maintains a persistent latent state evolving with each observation to adapt pretrained language models. This approach separates observation encoding, latent dynamics, and predictor adaptation, and is tested using deterministic formulations with a frozen GPT-2 small model.

In experiments on a four-turn hypothesis-inference task, the latent-gated LoRA method achieved 89.1% accuracy, comparable to 88.0% for a full-context LoRA baseline, despite relying solely on a 64-dimensional latent state for earlier evidence. Additional tests on a two-turn task with unseen codewords showed improved candidate ranking but limited exact codeword generation, indicating that persistent latent-conditioned adaptation can support sequential inference when prior context is unavailable.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.16375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models rely on finite token contexts, limiting access to earlier interactions. We introduce Recursive State-Augmented Language Models (Recursive SALM), a framework in which a persistent latent state evolves with each observation and generates adaptations of a pretrained language model. A modular read-transition-write architecture separates observation encoding, latent dynamics, and predictor adaptation. We develop deterministic and stochastic formulations. The experiments evaluate only deterministic SALM with frozen GPT-2 small and exclude earlier evidence from its decoder context. On a four-turn hypothesis-inference task, latent-gated LoRA reaches 89.1% accuracy, comparable to 88.0% for a trained full-context LoRA baseline, with earlier evidence available solely through a 64-dimensional state. Zeroing or shuffling the state substantially reduces accuracy. In a two-turn task with codewords unseen in training, several interfaces improve candidate ranking over chance, but rarely generate the exact codeword under the evaluated training schedule. These experiments show that persistent latent-conditioned adaptation can support sequential inference when earlier evidence is absent from the decoder context.

items.title: Researchers compare LoRA fine-tuning methods on Qwen3-8B for financial data, assessing task performance and generalization retention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reasoning Supervision and Capability Retention in LoRA Domain Adaptation
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated three low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning approaches on the Qwen3-8B model using financial data to improve task-specific performance without degrading generalization. They tested response-only LoRA, single-adapter reasoning with teacher model traces, and dual-adapter composite training, finding that response-only LoRA improved in-domain metrics while maintaining general capabilities near the frozen model's level.

The study showed that including reasoning traces in single-adapter or dual-adapter training did not surpass response-only LoRA in in-domain performance, though some benchmarks like MMLU-Pro saw slight improvements. Additionally, compressing teacher traces into shorter summaries shifted calibration metrics closer to response-only results but did not fully match them.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning foundation models on financial data has a wide range of applications, including identifying event types from news, monitoring risk and compliance language, and answering questions over filings and earnings calls. In this setting, the main challenge is to improve task performance without degrading the generalization capabilities of the model. In this paper, we present an extensive set of ablations for fine-tuning Qwen3-8B with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We compare three training regimes: (1) response-only LoRA, where the supervised response is the label alone; (2) single-adapter reasoning, where reasoning traces from a teacher model are included alongside the labels in the training loss; and (3) dual-adapter composite training, where separate LoRA adapters are trained on traces and labels. Response-only LoRA improves in-domain performance and leaves general capabilities near those of the frozen model. The in-domain change is largest for calibration and argmax accuracy. Under single-adapter reasoning, the in-domain metrics remain behind those of the response-only regime, while MMLU-Pro can rise slightly and the other retention benchmarks stay within ordinary variation. Dual-adapter composite training remains on the same side of this comparison and yields no further gain. Finally, we compress the teacher traces by summarizing them before training, and show that shorter summaries move calibration toward the response-only regime without reaching it.

items.title: Researchers present Metal Sandbox for isolated execution and command scheduling of GPU coding agents on Apple Silicon, achieving up to 2.14× throughput gains across interconnected Macs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Metal Sandbox: Isolated Execution and Command Scheduling for GPU Coding Agents on Apple Silicon
items.summary: Metal Sandbox is a new infrastructure designed to improve the efficiency of training and evaluating models that generate Apple Metal kernels by enabling isolated execution and command-level scheduling across multiple Mac mini M4 nodes. It allows concurrent parallel commands and manages serial commands with migration capabilities, integrating with Harbor for task execution and verification. Controlled experiments demonstrated throughput improvements between 1.68× and 2.05× under concentrated demand, with dynamic scheduling reducing tool waiting times and batch elapsed times significantly. The Metal Sandbox and Harbor integration are available as open-source on GitHub.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17294v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-device inference requires kernels that make effective use of local accelerators. Efficient training and evaluation of models that generate Apple Metal kernels benefit from native macOS tools and concurrent agent sessions. These sessions alternate between model requests, development commands, and GPU execution, leaving GPU capacity idle for much of a rollout. We present Metal Sandbox, infrastructure that combines restricted per-instance file access, native command execution, and command-level scheduling across interconnected Macs. Each agent retains its workspace and private development environment. Parallel commands can run concurrently, while serial commands share one execution slot per node; eligible waiting commands can migrate to available Macs and return results to the original agent. Integration with Harbor supports task execution, automatic verification, and rollout collection through a common workflow. Controlled experiments on four Mac mini M4 nodes achieve $1.68\times$--$2.05\times$ gains in command throughput under concentrated demand. Sixteen static agent traces give an estimated $2.14\times$ sustained-throughput gain for four sessions per node versus one, assuming continuously replenished sessions and unchanged mean durations. Replaying these measured traces under dynamic scheduling reduces mean tool waiting by 18.8% and batch elapsed time by 22.3%, assuming unchanged phase durations. Metal Sandbox and its Harbor integration are open-source on GitHub.

items.title: Fast-dLLM++ introduces Fréchet profile decoding to improve parallel token commitment in diffusion LLMs, boosting throughput by up to 37% with LLaDA-8B [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Fast-dLLM++: Fr\'echet Profile Decoding for Faster Diffusion LLM Inference
items.summary: Fast-dLLM++ is a training-free extension of Fast-dLLM that enhances diffusion large language model inference by selecting parallel commit sets based on the full sorted confidence profile rather than the weakest token's confidence. This approach generalizes previous decoding methods and exploits heterogeneous confidence profiles to increase safe parallelism without changing the underlying model or cache implementation. Experiments on benchmarks including GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, and MBPP with the LLaDA-8B model demonstrate that Fast-dLLM++ improves the accuracy-throughput trade-off, achieving up to 37% higher throughput at comparable accuracy. The method is a drop-in replacement for existing Fast-dLLM decoding and the code has been publicly released.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.02955v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion large language models promise parallel token generation, yet inference remains bottlenecked by deciding which masked tokens can be safely committed together. Fast-dLLM addressed this with KV caching and confidence-guided parallel decoding, but its decoding theory uses a homogeneous high-confidence assumption that effectively reduces each candidate set to its weakest selected token. We argue that this leaves speed on the table because real decoding steps exhibit heterogeneous confidence profiles. We propose Fast-dLLM++, a training-free extension that introduces Fr\'echet profile decoding: selecting parallel commit sets from the full sorted confidence profile rather than a single worst-case confidence. The resulting rule is a heterogeneous-confidence generalization of Fast-dLLM's factor selector and it recovers the previous rule exactly in the equal-confidence case and adds a provable heterogeneity bonus when the selected tokens have uneven confidences. Fast-dLLM++ leaves the model, diffusion process, and cache implementation entirely unchanged, making it a drop-in replacement for existing Fast-dLLM decoding. Experiments on GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, and MBPP with the LLaDA-8B model show that the theoretical improvement translates directly into empirical gains: profile-aware selection improves the accuracy-throughput frontier by exploiting safe parallelism that weakest-token rules miss, achieving up to 37% higher throughput at comparable accuracy. Our code release is at https://github.com/Ringo-Star/FastdLLM_plusplus.

items.title: Nemotron-Labs-Sigma introduces large-scale continuous diffusion language models with steerable latent trajectories, outperforming discrete models on reasoning and coding benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models
items.summary:
Nemotron-Labs-Sigma presents the first large-scale continuous diffusion language models (3B/8B parameters) using steerable, low-dimensional latent trajectories to improve reasoning and inference speed. These models leverage pretrained autoregressive weights and classifier-free guidance to achieve higher accuracy than state-of-the-art discrete diffusion and autoregressive baselines on benchmarks like GSM8K, Minerva, HumanEval, and MATH-500.

The continuous models enable efficient few-step distillation, providing up to 8x acceleration on math tasks and 4x on coding with minimal accuracy loss, and support one-step speculative decoding for further throughput gains. Their embedding-space steering allows control over the quality-diversity trade-off, establishing continuous diffusion language models as a promising approach for efficient language generation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.02665v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite the success of discrete diffusion language models (dLMs) for fast parallel decoding, their non-smooth, high-dimensional space hinders trajectory steering for reasoning and inference acceleration. To overcome this, we present Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, the first family of large-scale (3B/8B) continuous dLMs built on steerable, low-dimensional ODE/SDE latent trajectories. Trained blockwise via likelihood optimization, Nemotron-Labs-Sigma jointly denoises Gaussian-corrupted token embeddings while learning an optimal embedding geometry, and leverages pretrained autoregressive (AR) weights for warm-starting. At inference, we identify classifier-free guidance and score temperature as essential for high-fidelity reasoning and coding. Against state-of-the-art discrete counterparts (masked dLMs and AR baselines), Nemotron-Labs-Sigma outperforms them on standard benchmarks after pretraining (e.g., GSM8K, Minerva, HumanEval, MBPP) and on challenging reasoning tasks after supervised fine-tuning (e.g., MATH-500, AIME), with the largest consistent gains on coding. Beyond accuracy, we exploit two structural properties unique to continuous dLMs. First, smooth trajectories degrade gracefully at low NFEs and enable efficient few-step distillation: distribution matching proves strongest among the methods we study, giving roughly 8x acceleration on math and 4x on coding (8 and 4 tokens per forward pass) with negligible accuracy loss and preserved diversity. In addition, the one-step speculative decoding on the (pre-SFT) distilled 8B model yields a further ~3.5x throughput gain over the AR counterpart (on GB200), outperforming masked dLM baselines. Second, embedding-space steering controls the quality--diversity trade-off, yielding strong pass@$k$ that keeps improving as $k$ grows. Together, these results establish continuous dLMs as a promising paradigm for efficient language generation.

items.originalTitle: Unintended Side Effects of Value Training in LLMs
items.summary: Researchers adapted four instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) across Hofstede's cultural value dimensions to study how fine-tuning for specific values affects other capabilities and behaviors. They found that value-specific training led to unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits. The study suggests that post-training value alignment should include broader behavioral evaluations and highlights the need to determine the optimal stage for additional value training in the model pipeline. The researchers have released 48 value-tuned model checkpoints for further study.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.29922v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in value-sensitive contexts, aligning them with human values has emerged as a post-training objective in NLP, aimed at instilling additional values and guiding model behaviour. However, current evaluations remain narrow. Because values are interconnected, it is unclear how fine-tuning for specific values alters unrelated capabilities and behaviours. In this work, we adapt four instruction-tuned LLMs across individual Hofstede's value dimensions and evaluate them on both cross-value transfer and broader behaviours. We find that value-specific training produces unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits. Consequently, we suggest that value alignment after post-training should incorporate broader behavioral evaluations, and we highlight the need to investigate where additional value training might best fit into the pipeline. We release all 48 value-tuned model checkpoints at https://huggingface.co/sidicity/cultural-value-models

items.originalTitle: An Experimental Study of Hybrid Retrieval, NLI and Open-source LLMs for Scientific Claim Verification
items.summary: Researchers conducted an experimental study to evaluate scientific claim verification methods using a benchmark of 2,035 claims from SciFact and CliniFact datasets. They compared a DeBERTa-based NLI model against open-source large language models (LLMs) including Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B, using a hybrid retrieval approach combining semantic and lexical methods to select relevant evidence sentences. Qwen3 achieved the highest Macro-F1 score of 0.7937, outperforming Llama 3.1 and Mistral, while the NLI baseline scored 0.3157.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.03093v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Claim verification is the task of deciding whether a source text supports a claim, contradicts it, or lacks sufficient evidence. Natural Language Inference (NLI) models can judge whether a single sentence supports or contradicts a claim, but they struggle when the evidence is spread across several sentences. Conversely, Large Language Models (LLMs) can reason across sentences, but may draw conclusions the text does not support. In this experimental study, we test whether a conservative fusion rule, labeling a claim Support or Contradict only when both models agree and defaulting to Not Enough Evidence otherwise, combines their strengths. We construct a benchmark of 2,035 claims from SciFact and CliniFact (858 Support, 152 Contradict, 1,025 Not Enough Evidence). We retrieve the top five most relevant sentences per claim using a hybrid of semantic and lexical (BM25) retrieval, which slightly outperforms either method alone. These retrieved sentences are then provided to every verification model. We then compare a DeBERTa-v3-base-mnli-fever-anli NLI baseline against Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B. Qwen3 achieves the highest Macro-F1 (0.7937), followed by Llama 3.1 (0.7204) and Mistral (0.6388), while the NLI baseline reaches only 0.3157. Contrary to our hypothesis, fusion degrades performance, dropping Macro-F1 to 0.7392, 0.6730, and 0.5991, respectively. To understand this decline, we analyze agreements, disagreements, and common error patterns between the NLI and LLM verifiers. Our error analysis shows that NLI and LLM disagreements often result in correct LLM predictions being overturned.

items.title: Researchers introduce NaijaFacts benchmark to separate language proficiency from factual knowledge in AI models across Nigerian languages and compare with US/UK data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: NaijaFacts: A Framework for Disentangling Language from Knowledge in Facts about Nigeria
items.summary: Researchers developed NaijaFacts, a benchmark of factual and statistical questions about Nigeria in English, Nigerian Pidgin, Yorùbá, Igbo, and Hausa, to evaluate whether AI models truly know facts about Africa rather than just language skills. They compared model performance on similar questions about the UK and US to distinguish between language effects and knowledge gaps, finding that knowledge gaps dominate, with much lower accuracy on Nigerian statistics than on US/UK data. The study also extended to all 54 African countries, revealing a continent-wide pattern of high accuracy on cultural and political questions but low accuracy on statistical facts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.06504v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multilingual benchmarks for African languages mostly translate generic questions into local languages, measuring linguistic competence but not whether models know facts about Africa. We introduce NaijaFacts, a benchmark of factual and statistical questions about Nigeria, authored by native speakers and grounded in authoritative official statistics, with every question available in English, Nigerian Pidgin, Yor\`ub\'a, Igbo, and Hausa. Answering similar questions for the UK and US yields a country by language matrix that disentangles a language effect (the model knows the fact but degrades in a low-resource language) from a knowledge effect (the fact is absent in every language). Across eight frontier and Nigeria-adapted models, the knowledge effect dominates: English-query accuracy is 49-50% for the US/UK but 20% for Nigeria. The language effect is smaller and tracks web representation, degrading from English to Yor\`ub\'a (9 points on Nigeria, up to 24 on US/UK questions). We find scale does not help: the strongest models reach 66-79% on the UK and the US but none exceed 31% on Nigerian statistics. Extending to all 54 African countries with our best performing frontier model shows the same profile continent-wide, 96% on culture and 98% on politics against 26% on statistics, so the gap is not specific to Nigeria.

items.title: Researchers compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, finding label-wording augmentation improves accuracy on unfamiliar words but not on abbreviations or codes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated two versions of Ru-Jev, a multilingual cross-encoder trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks, to assess the impact of label wording on model accuracy. The later release introduced label-wording augmentation presenting labels in multiple surface forms, which improved accuracy on held-out vocabularies containing ordinary or borrowed words such as jargon and office slang, but showed no significant gains on abbreviations or opaque codes.

The study tested ten label vocabularies with varying candidate sizes and controlled for overlap with training data. Some accuracy gains depended on a single label rarely chosen by the earlier release, and adjusting for per-option biases reduced these gains except for jargon. On datasets unseen during training, accuracy changes varied, and rankings of training checkpoints disagreed, indicating challenges in checkpoint selection. The researchers also identified four evaluation hazards when comparing the two releases.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08439v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies at five and eighteen candidates, checked for overlap with the training data. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release has higher point accuracy in all fourteen cells, by up to 0.24. Several of these gains rest partly on one label that the earlier release almost never chose; fitting one bias per option removes part of them, while the jargon gain largely survives. On abbreviations and opaque codes the augmented release gives no usable gain: its loss on 17 abbreviations unrelated to training (-0.060) is one label and disappears after the same correction. The comparison is between two trained releases, not a controlled ablation, and the earlier recipe varies across seeds by up to 0.098 on the strictest slice. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points, narrowed to -3.4 and +1.4 by the per-option biases; on a third, scientific rubrics, the augmented release is ahead of both runs of the earlier recipe after the correction. Rankings of ten training checkpoints disagree across the three unseen datasets, so none of them should choose the checkpoint. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.
