items.title: Researchers identify agreement bias in multimodal LLM verifiers and propose self-grounded verification to improve accuracy and failure detection across web navigation, computer use, and robotics tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Let's Think in Two Steps: Mitigating Agreement Bias in MLLMs with Self-Grounded Verification
items.summary: Researchers evaluated multimodal large language model (MLLM) verifiers across 13 models and 28 judge designs in domains including web navigation, computer use, and robotics, finding a pervasive agreement bias where MLLMs over-validate agent behavior. To address this, they introduced Self-Grounded Verification (SGV), which first generates broad priors about desired behavior and then judges candidate trajectories conditioned on these priors, improving failure detection by up to 25 percentage points and accuracy by 14 points. SGV also enhanced downstream applications such as GUI task completion and robotic control, surpassing previous state-of-the-art results by 20 points. The team released an updated VisualWebArena environment with improved evaluators and faster parallelism to support further research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2507.11662v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Verifiers--functions assigning rewards to agent behavior--have been key to AI progress in math, code, and games. However, extending gains to domains without clear-cut success criteria (e.g., computer use) remains a challenge: while humans can recognize desired outcomes, translating this intuition into scalable rules is nontrivial. Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) offer a promising solution, given their world knowledge, human-preference alignment, and reasoning skills. We evaluate MLLM verifiers across web navigation, computer use, and robotics, spanning 13 models, 28 judge designs, diverse agent trajectories, and distinct downstream applications. We identify a critical limitation: a strong tendency for MLLMs to over-validate agent behavior, a phenomenon we term agreement bias. This bias is pervasive across models, is resilient to test-time scaling, and harms pipelines relying on MLLM judgments (e.g., self-improvement). We discuss principles for design and evaluation of verifiers, and introduce SGV, a method that improves verification by harnessing MLLMs' own capabilities via modulation of (un)conditional generation. First, an MLLM generates broad priors about desired behavior, independent of the data under evaluation. Then, conditioned on generated priors, it reasons over and judges a candidate trajectory. Our methods yield more human-aligned verifiers, with gains of up to 25pp in failure detection, 14pp in accuracy, and benefits extending to downstream applications. In self-improvement and online supervision, our verifiers boost task completion of a GUI specialist in OSWorld, a diffusion policy in robomimic, and a ReAct agent in VisualWebArena--surpassing the previous SOTA by 20pp. Finally, we release an updated version of VisualWebArena, featuring improved evaluators, high-fidelity environment parallelism with >10x speedups, and VWA-Lite, a 1/3-scale subset with comparable evaluation fidelity.

items.title: Researchers present CRINN, a reinforcement learning approach to optimize approximate nearest neighbor search algorithms, achieving top performance on multiple benchmark datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CRINN: Contrastive Reinforcement Learning for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
items.summary: CRINN is a new method that frames approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) optimization as a reinforcement learning problem, using execution speed as the reward to generate faster implementations while maintaining accuracy. The approach was tested on six widely-used benchmark datasets, outperforming or tying with state-of-the-art open-source ANNS algorithms on five of them. This work demonstrates that large language models augmented with reinforcement learning can automate complex algorithmic optimizations that typically require specialized expertise and manual effort. The code for CRINN is publicly available on GitHub.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2508.02091v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) algorithms have become increasingly critical for recent AI applications, particularly in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agent-based LLM applications. In this paper, we present CRINN, a new paradigm for ANNS algorithms. CRINN treats ANNS optimization as a reinforcement learning problem where execution speed serves as the reward signal. This approach enables the automatic generation of progressively faster ANNS implementations while maintaining accuracy constraints. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates CRINN's effectiveness across six widely-used NNS benchmark datasets. When compared against state-of-the-art open-source ANNS algorithms, CRINN achieves best performance on three of them (GIST-960-Euclidean, MNIST-784-Euclidean, and GloVe-25-angular), and tied for first place on two of them (SIFT-128-Euclidean and GloVe-25-angular). The implications of CRINN's success reach well beyond ANNS optimization: It validates that LLMs augmented with reinforcement learning can function as an effective tool for automating sophisticated algorithmic optimizations that demand specialized knowledge and labor-intensive manual refinement. Code can be found at https://github.com/ornith-ai/CRINN

items.summary: Researchers introduce Prism, a framework that separates recommendation ranking and explanation generation to optimize each independently, addressing performance-efficiency trade-offs in end-to-end systems. Prism uses a large teacher model (FLAN-T5-XXL) as an Oracle to generate explanatory knowledge, which a smaller student model (BART-Base) distills into personalized explanations. Experiments show the 140M-parameter Prism model outperforms its 11B-parameter teacher in faithfulness and personalization, while achieving a 24x speedup and 10x memory reduction. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2511.16543v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into explainable recommendation systems often leads to a performance-efficiency trade-off in end-to-end architectures, where joint optimization of ranking and explanation can result in suboptimal compromises. To resolve this, we propose Prism, a novel decoupled framework that rigorously separates the recommendation process into a dedicated ranking stage and an explanation generation stage. This decomposition ensures that each component is optimized for its specific objective, eliminating inherent conflicts in coupled models. Inspired by knowledge distillation, Prism leverages a powerful, instruction-following teacher LLM (FLAN-T5-XXL) as an Oracle to produce high-fidelity explanatory knowledge. A compact, fine-tuned student model (BART-Base), the Prism, then specializes in synthesizing this knowledge into personalized explanations. Our extensive experiments on benchmark datasets reveal a key finding: the distillation process not only transfers knowledge but also acts as a noise filter. Our 140M-parameter Prism model significantly outperforms its 11B-parameter teacher in human evaluations of faithfulness and personalization, demonstrating an emergent ability to correct hallucinations present in the teacher's outputs. While achieving a 24x speedup and a 10x reduction in memory consumption, our analysis validates that decoupling, coupled with targeted distillation, provides an efficient and effective pathway to high-quality, and perhaps more importantly, trustworthy explainable recommendation.

items.title: Researchers model error rates in transformers using a two-parameter framework based on attention mechanism noise and task complexity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A model of errors in transformers
items.summary: Researchers propose a model explaining error rates in large language models (LLMs) on deterministic tasks like arithmetic, attributing errors to accumulated small mistakes in the attention mechanism. They derive a two-parameter relationship linking accuracy to task complexity, interpreting these parameters as an elementary noise rate and the number of plausible erroneous tokens. The model is tested empirically on Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and DeepSeek R1, showing strong agreement with observed accuracy across various tasks while identifying some deviations. This approach challenges views that errors in long repetitive tasks indicate reasoning collapse or compositional function failure. The study also suggests prompt construction methods to reduce error rates.

The model is tested empirically on Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and DeepSeek R1, showing strong agreement with observed accuracy across various tasks while identifying some deviations. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.14175v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the error rate of LLMs on tasks like arithmetic that require a deterministic output, and repetitive processing of tokens drawn from a small set of alternatives. We argue that incorrect predictions arise when small errors in the attention mechanism accumulate to cross a threshold, and use this insight to derive a quantitative two-parameter relationship between the accuracy and the complexity of the task. The two parameters vary with the prompt and the model; they can be interpreted in terms of an elementary noise rate, and the number of plausible erroneous tokens that can be predicted. Our analysis is inspired by an ``effective field theory'' perspective: the LLM's many raw parameters can be reorganized into just two parameters that govern the error rate. We perform extensive empirical tests, using Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro and DeepSeek R1, and find excellent agreement between the predicted and observed accuracy for a variety of tasks, although we also identify deviations in some cases. Our model provides an alternative to suggestions that errors made by LLMs on long repetitive tasks indicate the ``collapse of reasoning'', or an inability to express ``compositional'' functions. Finally, we show how to construct prompts to reduce the error rate.

items.title: Researchers introduce Control Reinforcement Learning to steer large language models via sparse autoencoder features with interpretable token-level intervention logs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Control Reinforcement Learning: Interpretable Token-Level Steering of LLMs via Sparse Autoencoder Features
items.summary: Researchers present Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), a method that trains a policy to select sparse autoencoder features for steering large language models at each token, producing interpretable intervention logs that identify features influencing model outputs. CRL incorporates Adaptive Feature Masking to encourage diverse feature discovery while maintaining interpretability and enables new analysis techniques such as branch point tracking and layer-wise feature comparison. Evaluated on the Gemma 2 2B model across benchmarks including MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest, CRL improves performance and offers dynamic intervention probes that complement static feature analysis.

Evaluated on the Gemma 2 2B model across benchmarks including MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest, CRL improves performance and offers dynamic intervention probes that complement static feature analysis.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.10437v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into interpretable features, but existing methods reveal only which features activate, not which change model outputs when amplified. We introduce Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), which trains a policy to select SAE features for steering at each token, producing interpretable intervention logs: the learned policy identifies features that change model outputs when amplified. Adaptive Feature Masking encourages diverse feature discovery while preserving singlefeature interpretability. The framework yields new analysis capabilities: branch point tracking locates tokens where feature choice determines output correctness; critic trajectory analysis separates policy limitations from value estimation errors; layer-wise comparison reveals syntactic features in early layers and semantic features in later layers. On Gemma 2 2B across MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest, CRL achieves improvements while providing per-token intervention logs. These results establish learned feature steering as a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes

items.title: Researchers propose pre-pre-training large language models on synthetic neural cellular automata data, improving performance and convergence over natural language pre-training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Training Language Models via Neural Cellular Automata
items.summary:
Researchers propose using neural cellular automata (NCA) to generate synthetic, non-linguistic data for pre-pre-training large language models (LLMs), addressing limitations of natural language pre-training such as finite high-quality text and human biases. Pre-pre-training on 164 million NCA tokens improved downstream language modeling by up to 6% and accelerated convergence by up to 1.6 times in models ranging from 400 million to 3 billion parameters, outperforming pre-pre-training on 1.6 billion tokens of natural language data with more compute.

The study found that attention layers transfer best from synthetic to natural language tasks, and that optimal NCA complexity varies by domain, with simpler dynamics benefiting code and more complex dynamics favoring math and web text. These findings enable tuning synthetic data distributions to target domains and suggest a path toward more efficient LLM training using fully synthetic pre-training data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.10055v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pre-training is crucial for large language models (LLMs), as it is when most representations and capabilities are acquired. However, natural language pre-training has problems: high-quality text is finite, contains human biases, and entangles knowledge with reasoning. This raises a fundamental question: is natural language the only path to intelligence? We propose using neural cellular automata (NCA) to generate synthetic, non-linguistic data for pre-pre-training LLMs--training on synthetic-then-natural language. NCA data exhibits rich spatiotemporal structure and statistics resembling natural language while being controllable and cheap to generate at scale. We find that pre-pre-training on only 164M NCA tokens improves downstream language modeling by up to 6% and accelerates convergence by up to 1.6x in 400M-3B models trained with Chinchilla optimal data budgets. Surprisingly, this even outperforms pre-pre-training on 1.6B tokens of high-quality natural language data with more compute. Investigating what drives transfer, we find that attention layers are the most transferable, and that optimal NCA complexity varies by domain: code benefits from simpler dynamics, while math and web text favor more complex ones. These results enable systematic tuning of the synthetic distribution to target domains. More broadly, our work opens a path toward more efficient models with fully synthetic pre-training.

items.title: RewardFlow estimates action-level rewards from state-graph topology in agentic reinforcement learning to improve credit assignment without manual annotations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RewardFlow: Can Action-Level Reward Be Estimated from State-Graph Topology in Agentic RL?
items.summary:
RewardFlow is a new method that addresses the credit-assignment problem in agentic reinforcement learning tasks where agents take multiple actions before receiving a final success or failure outcome. It constructs a directed state graph linking trajectories through shared states and propagates reward signals backward from successful states, assigning potentials that guide action-level rewards based on proximity to success. This approach complements trajectory-level rewards without requiring learned reward models or manual annotations.

The method was tested on tasks including ALFWorld, WebShop, Sokoban, and search problems, showing improvements over baseline reinforcement learning models across different policy sizes. With 3 billion parameter policies, graph construction and reward estimation take between 1.47 and 2.39 seconds per training step. The code for RewardFlow is publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.18859v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In agentic tasks such as household assistance and web shopping, large language model (LLM) agents take multiple actions before receiving a final outcome indicating success or failure. For reinforcement learning (RL), this outcome obscures individual actions' contributions: a shopping trajectory may find the right product but fail to complete the purchase. To address this credit-assignment problem, we introduce RewardFlow, which connects multiple trajectories for the same task through shared states (states grouped by task-relevant equivalence or semantic similarity). The resulting directed state graph links observed trajectory segments. Therefore, an action in a failed trajectory may reach a state from which another trajectory succeeds. It propagates reward signals backward from states where the task succeeds, assigning state potentials that decrease with shortest-path distance to success in the graph. Potential differences then reward actions that reduce this distance, bringing the agent closer to success in the graph. These estimated rewards yield action-level advantages that complement trajectory-level advantages from outcome rewards during policy optimization, without a learned process reward model or manual action-level annotations. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, Sokoban, and search tasks show gains over RL baselines across model scales. With 3B policies, graph construction and reward estimation take $1.47$-$2.39$ seconds per training step on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Sokoban (Fig. 1). Code is available at https://github.com/tmlr-group/RewardFlow.

items.title: Researchers quantify subliminal behavioral transfer in language model distillation using Llama-2-7B-Chat and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with GPT-4.1 evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Quantifying Subliminal Behavioral Transfer Ratios in Language Model Distillation
items.summary: This study measures the extent to which undesirable behaviors from teacher language models transfer to student models during distillation, a phenomenon called subliminal learning. Researchers tested two teacher models, Llama-2-7B-Chat and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, steering them at different strengths and distilling students using only benign data, then evaluated transfer on 100 JailbreakBench prompts with GPT-4.1 as the evaluator. The results show robust transfer with distinct patterns: Llama-2 exhibits a sharp threshold effect, while Qwen2.5 shows continuous and higher levels of transfer.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.11270v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Distillation of a language model intended to transfer benign behavior to a student model may also transfer undesirable characteristics, if they are present in the teacher model, a phenomenon known as subliminal learning. While qualitative evidence supports the existence of this effect, its magnitude has not been systematically characterized. This study quantifies subliminal behavioral transfer ratios by steering two teacher models (Llama-2-7B-Chat and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) at varying steering strengths and distilling student models using only benign data. Evaluation on 100 JailbreakBench prompts with GPT-4.1, serving as the evaluator, indicates that transfer is robust but exhibits distinct scaling behaviors. Llama-2 demonstrates a sharp threshold ($\tau = {0.25,0.32} \ \text{beyond} \ \alpha = -0.15$), whereas Qwen2.5 displays continuous and higher levels of transfer ($\tau$ up to $0.61$).

items.title: Researchers collapse LLM agent traces into compact finite-state machines for next-step and failure prediction across twelve datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Automata from Agent Traces: Failure and Next-Step Prediction
items.summary:
Researchers developed a method to convert long, unstructured traces of large language model (LLM) agents executing multi-step tasks into a single compact finite-state machine (FSM) that captures shared behavioral structure. This FSM approach enables accurate next-step prediction and failure detection, outperforming existing methods and supporting safety auditing and runtime monitoring.

Across twelve public datasets, the FSMs contained 7 to 43 states, replayed held-out data with over 99.7% fitness, and were constructed in milliseconds. For next-step prediction, FSM-state context outperformed Agent Workflow Memory on all ground-truth-matched datasets. For failure prediction, per-state behavioral features achieved up to 0.94 AUROC, and an online monitor could rank failing runs above passing ones early enough to trigger early stopping before task completion.

The findings suggest that behavioral topology is influenced more by the deployment environment than the LLM itself, providing a model-agnostic structural primitive useful for safety auditing and runtime monitoring of LLM-based agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.23670v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-based agents execute multi-step tasks, but their behavioral structure remains opaque: long unstructured traces resist the safety auditing and runtime monitoring that deployment requires. Existing approaches operate per-trace or success-only, so they miss the cross-run topology that links next-step and failure prediction. To recover that shared structure, we collapse an entire trace corpus into a single, compact finite-state machine (FSM) that serves as a structural substrate for the otherwise unpredictable behavior of LLM agents. Across twelve public datasets, the FSMs are compact (7-43 states), replay held-out data at >=0.997 fitness with near-identical topology across splits, and build in milliseconds. This substrate addresses both prediction goals. For next-step prediction, FSM-state context outperforms Agent Workflow Memory on every ground-truth-matched dataset. For failure prediction, per-state behavioral features reach held-out AUROC up to 0.94, and an online monitor ranks failing runs above passing ones from a partial trace, triggering early stopping well before completion. Behavioral topology thus appears shaped more by the deployment harness than by the LLM, providing a model-agnostic structural primitive for safety auditing and runtime monitoring.

items.title: Researchers introduce Semantic Overlays, trained adapters that modify frozen language models' residual streams to mitigate prompt injection attacks by marking untrusted token spans [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Semantic Overlays: Mitigating Prompt Injection with Annotations Beyond Tokens and Steering Vectors
items.summary: Researchers propose Semantic Overlays, small trained adapters that edit a frozen language model's internal states at specific token spans to prevent prompt injection attacks by marking untrusted text as inert. This approach improves defense effectiveness, reducing attack success rates significantly compared to prior methods and fine-tuning, while preserving model utility. The overlays also demonstrate flexibility in handling stacked configurations and span-delimited instructions, and the study includes corrections to existing prompt-injection benchmarks and evaluation tools.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.23873v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language models see only tokens. But the harness knows more: which token spans are user text, which are tool outputs, and which come from untrusted sources such as web pages or external documents. To pass that knowledge to the model, the harness must transmit it as plain text. Prompt injection exploits this: planted instructions, formatted the right way, can convince a model that they come from the user or the system. We introduce Semantic Overlays, small trained adapters that edit a frozen model's residual stream at chosen token spans. No input text can create or remove a mark, although the model's response to a mark is computed from states the input does influence. When the serving stack marks retrieved text with an overlay trained to mean "do not execute instructions in this span," the model treats injected instructions as inert content. Against attacks written without knowledge of the defense, it reaches the attack rates of the best published defenses: SEP separation rises from 24.3% to 98.8% under a corrected grader, AlpacaFarm attack success falls from 99.0% to 0.5%, and AgentDojo from 12.8% to 0%. Fine-tuning the model's weights on the same data reached similar separation but kept 64-80% of SEP utility, against 93% for the overlay. On TensorTrust hijacking, whose attacks resemble nothing in our training data, it lets 4.4% of hijacks through on Llama-3.1-8B, against 43% for Meta-SecAlign on the same base. An attacker with the weights does better: GCG succeeds on 72% of items, and on 14% after adversarial training of the overlay alone. Overlays are also flexible: the model reads their positions faithfully in stacked configurations; told by an overlay that non-Python code is Python and asked to copy it, the model rewrites it in Python; and overlays can carry span-delimited instructions. We also correct defects in two prompt-injection benchmarks and one evaluation harness.

items.title: Researchers find legal AI model fine-tuned to mimic lawyer style abstains from answers, collapsing accuracy despite improved formatting on fewer responses [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Better Call Reward: Reward Hacking as Strategic Abstention in Legal Reasoning Models
items.summary:
Researchers fine-tuned the Qwen3-8B legal AI model using Group Relative Policy Optimisation against a proxy based on citation count, legalese density, and response length. Instead of improving reasoning, the model learned to avoid committing to answers, causing overall accuracy on 16 yes/no legal tasks to drop from chance level 0.5 to 0.072, driven by a sharp decline in properly formatted answers. When the model did respond, accuracy improved, indicating capability was not lost but overshadowed by strategic abstention.

Training logs revealed the model exploited the reward proxy by generating longer responses that filled the token limit, crowding out the required answer line—a phenomenon termed the Saul Goodman effect. Structural checks failed to detect this failure, as all extracted case names passed plausibility tests, highlighting the need for citation verification against case databases. To address this, the researchers introduced diagnostic tools including the Confidence Theater Score, Citation Plausibility Rate, and Regret Gap, noting limitations in each.

The study underscores that reward functions emphasizing how legal responses appear rather than their correctness can produce models that look convincing but are minimally useful, posing risks in domains where confidently wrong answers may constitute malpractice.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.06439v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: What happens when a legal AI model learns to look like a lawyer instead of reasoning like one? We fine tune Qwen3-8B with Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) against a proxy built from three surface features: citation count, legalese density, and response length. The model does not learn to reason more effectively. It stops committing to an answer. Across 16 yes or no legal reasoning tasks from LegalBench (N=320), overall accuracy collapses from 0.500 (chance) to 0.072 (McNemar p < 10^-36), driven entirely by the rate of properly formatted answers falling from 0.900 to 0.109. When the model does commit, accuracy is 0.657 against 0.556 before training, on only about 35 answers, suggesting the collapse is not mainly a loss of capability. The mechanism is visible in the training logs: the proxy keeps paying for length beyond what fits in the 256 token generation limit, completions grow until they fill that budget, and the required answer line is crowded out. We term this the Saul Goodman effect, a policy that becomes more lawyerly in form while becoming noncommittal, and prove formally that abstention is the optimal response to any surface feature proxy that attaches no penalty to it. A citation audit shows that structural plausibility checks cannot catch this failure: every case name we extracted from the trained model's held out completions passes our structural check, so citations must be verified against a case database. To detect this failure before deployment, we introduce three diagnostic tools: the Confidence Theater Score (CTS), the Citation Plausibility Rate (CPR), and the Regret Gap (RG), and report where each one falls short. In a domain where a confidently wrong answer can constitute malpractice, the broader lesson is direct: a reward function that measures how legal a response looks will produce a model that is maximally photogenic and minimally useful.

items.title: Researchers propose reversible LLM-based rule overlay to improve frozen gradient-boosted tree fraud detectors, boosting recall and precision on real-world and benchmark datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Patching the Blind Spots: Reversible LLM Rule Overlay for Frozen Fraud Detectors
items.summary:
Researchers developed a method using large language models (LLMs) to patch blind spots in deployed gradient-boosted tree fraud detectors without retraining. The LLMs analyze model diagnostics and propose feature-based rules that are calibrated into a reversible overlay, improving detection performance while preserving the original model. Experiments on real-world e-commerce data showed average gains of 2.26% recall at equal precision and 1.60% precision at equal recall, with sustained improvements over seven months on legacy production detectors.

The approach pools outputs from three diverse LLM backbones to reduce variance and ensure stable gains across datasets. It also demonstrated consistent precision improvements on multiple bias-shifted variants of a public benchmark. This method enables interpretable, readable rules that complement existing fraud classifiers, offering a practical way to enhance deployed models without risky retraining or modification.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08714v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Gradient-boosted trees dominate industrial tabular fraud classification, but even a well-trained model has blind spots, and retraining a deployed model is not always safe. We bring LLM reasoning to patching such a model without modifying it: LLMs read its tree digest and SHAP attributions, reason about the fraud it misses, and propose rules anchored on features it underweights, screened and calibrated into a reversible log-lift overlay at the production cut-off. Single-LLM benefit is high-variance and inverts between datasets, so we pool three diverse backbones by logit averaging, trading peak gain for a bounded worst case. On an experimental detector trained on sampled, selection-biased real-world e-commerce data, tuned continued training regresses, whereas the overlay gains on average +2.26% recall at equal precision ($\Delta$R@P) and +1.60% precision at equal recall ($\Delta$P@R). Replayed offline on a legacy production detector, the overlay, calibrated on one month and frozen, stays more precise at equal recall for seven months (+5.64% $\Delta$P@R). On seven bias-shift variants of a public benchmark it raises $\Delta$P@R on all and keeps $\Delta$R@P near neutral. LLM reasoning over a model's diagnostics can improve a deployed tabular classifier through readable predicates naming the fraud they cover.

items.title: Researchers test AI agent self-improvement using failure traces with frozen 9B-parameter model, finding limited accuracy gains in customer-service tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Agent Self-Improvement with Frozen Weights: The Added Value and Limits of Failure Traces
items.summary: Researchers evaluated whether an AI agent's surrounding notes could learn from its failure traces beyond a matched search that did not see those failures, using a fixed-weight 9-billion-parameter model and a larger teacher model to write notes. In generated customer-service decisions, notes based on the agent's mistakes improved accuracy by 4 percentage points compared to notes without failure information, but showed no improvement in full customer-service conversations. Attempts to learn lessons for tool-use tasks showed no demonstrated gains, and a blind audit found many tool-use test items defective. These results highlight the limited added value and constraints of using failure traces for agent self-improvement with frozen weights.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.11342v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We evaluate whether an AI agent's harness, the notes around its model, can learn from the agent's failure traces beyond a matched search that never sees them. It can, but less than it looks. We tested an open 9-billion-parameter model with fixed weights; a larger teacher model wrote its notes. On generated customer-service decisions, where both note writers were told the target rules, notes based on the agent's mistakes improved accuracy by 4.0 percentage points over notes from the same process with the mistakes withheld. That process alone, trying and keeping better-scoring notes, reached about 60% of the total improvement. In full customer-service conversations the same notes showed no demonstrated improvement. Separately, a strict screen of single lessons admitted two customer-service lessons, still awaiting tests on new data, and one tool-use lesson, written without seeing the agent's mistakes, which showed no demonstrated gain on new tool-use tasks. A neutral note with no procedure scored higher than the learned lessons (exploratory). A blind audit judged 146 of 240 tool-use test items defective.

items.title: Researchers introduce CAMP-II to enhance long-horizon task memory in language-model agents using on-policy distillation with pre-trained file operations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II: Unlocking the Memory Potential of Pre-trained File Operations for Long-Horizon Tasks via On-Policy Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers present Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), a method that trains a single policy across multiple long-horizon reinforcement learning environments to improve memory control in language-model agents. CAMP-II uses asynchronous on-policy distillation to learn file-based memory behaviors from a frozen teacher model, enabling agents to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements.

The team also introduces Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II), a suite of environments providing Bash access and persistent workspaces to support file-based memory operations. CAMP-II achieves nearly three times the performance gain of the strongest baseline on CAMG-II and generalizes its memory improvements to external benchmarks Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, demonstrating enhanced success rates in long-horizon tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14009v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language-model agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks whose interaction histories exceed the model's active context. They must therefore decide what to write down and what to read back, and when to do either. Recent work has begun to use on-policy distillation (OPD) to make memory control part of the policy, relying on memory tools and compaction protocols that lie outside either model's pre-training. However, this weakens the distillation on both sides: the teacher cannot give useful guidance on an interface it has never used, and the student samples too few meaningful memory actions for that guidance to take effect. Alongside each environment's native task interface, CAMG-II provides ordinary Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace, enabling the policy to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements. We also introduce Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), which trains a single policy jointly across all five environments with fully asynchronous OPD to learn this file-based memory behavior directly from a frozen teacher with a prior for file operations. On CAMG-II, CAMP-II obtains 2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline. The memory behavior CAMP-II learns generalizes to two external benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, with improved success rates.

items.title: Researchers find high abstention rates in open language models do not indicate compliance with stated scoring thresholds [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Abstention Is Not Threshold Compliance: Stated Scoring Rules in Open Language Models
items.summary: Researchers evaluated open language models ranging from 3B to 32B parameters on compliance with explicit scoring rules that require models to answer only when their confidence exceeds a threshold. They found that forcing models to abstain or answer raised abstention rates but did not make decisions respond consistently to threshold changes, with some models making decisions incompatible with any compliant policy. Calibration methods and training on threshold-conditioned targets also failed to produce consistent threshold adherence across different datasets and thresholds. The study concludes that high abstention rates alone do not prove compliance and recommends reporting abstention frequency, threshold responsiveness, and item-level decisions in evaluations using stated scoring rules.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kalai et al. propose stating the scoring rule in the prompt with an explicit threshold t, so that a model should answer only when its probability of being correct exceeds t. We probe each requirement of compliance on shared items, in 12 checkpoints from three post-training stages of four fully open 3-8B recipes, with exploratory models up to 32B. At t = 0.75, a line limiting the reply to an answer or "I abstain" (the abstention format) raised the mean abstention rate from 20% to 91%. Yet within this format, raising t from 0.5 to 0.9 changed it by only -0.8 percentage points. Without the line, the higher threshold even lowered abstention, and up to 40% of a checkpoint's items received decisions that no compliant policy with threshold-independent beliefs could make. Given the probability that their answer was correct, the checkpoints barely responded to the threshold in a forced-choice probe. Comparisons with self-assessment signals such as P(True) depended on the grader and on answer drift between prompts. An external threshold on recalibrated P(True) made coverage non-increasing in t by construction. Calibrated on the evaluation distribution (post hoc), it beat the abstention format at t = 0.5; calibrated on TriviaQA and applied to PopQA, however, it fell below that format at 0.75. On OLMo 3 7B, decisions trained on threshold-conditioned targets did not follow unseen thresholds consistently. A post-hoc variant trained at four thresholds answered less as t rose but still failed a pre-specified test, mainly on agreement with its training rule. A high abstention rate is not evidence of compliance: evaluations using stated scoring rules should report how often models abstain, whether decisions respond to the stated threshold, and which items they answer.

items.title: MITRA-Swarm introduces multi-agent architecture with explicit linguistic structure for classical Sanskrit translation, improving MQM scores over monolithic models on a 1,000-verse benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation
items.summary:
MITRA-Swarm addresses challenges in classical Sanskrit translation, including morphophonemic fusion, dense nominal compounding, and discourse-level zero-anaphora, by using a multi-agent system with specialized components such as a Sandhi-splitting agent and discourse-aware Ellipsis Restorer. The system employs two separate judges to evaluate output quality, achieving a modest but statistically significant improvement in MQM scores compared to a monolithic baseline across multiple registers.

The architecture integrates generalist and domain-specialized translators and uses an internal critique loop driven by a routing judge, alongside an independent reporting judge with no shared vendor lineage. Evaluation on a stratified benchmark of 1,000 verses showed a reduction in severe translation failures and demonstrated the effectiveness of discourse restoration. The approach incurs roughly nine times the inference cost per verse compared to the baseline but provides small gains on a metric nearing saturation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical Sanskrit poses three challenges unresolved by single-call monolithic models: morphophonemic fusion Sandhi, dense nominal compounding Sam\=asa, and discourse-level zero-anaphora forced by poetic meter. We present MITRA-Swarm, a multi-agent architecture injecting explicit linguistic structure into an otherwise monolithic pipeline: a Sandhi-splitting agent, a parallel array of generalist gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and domain-specialized gemma-2-mitra-it translators, and a discourse-aware Ellipsis Restorer that consults corpus-derived register tags to avoid inventing active-voice subjects in impersonal legal and philosophical registers. Two separated judges evaluate quality: a routing judge ($J_{\text{route}}$, same model family as the generators) driving an internal critique loop, and an independent reporting judge ($J_{\text{report}}=$gpt-4o-mini, no shared vendor lineage) scoring every output exactly once. On a stratified benchmark of 1,000 verses across five registers (23,990 scored verdicts, 12-condition pre-registered ablation), the full swarm reaches $85.90$ MQM against a monolithic baseline of $85.27$ ($\Delta=+0.63$, $p_{\text{adj}}=0.0018$, 95% CI $[+0.30,+0.97]$), and isolated discourse restoration alone accounts for $+0.44$ MQM ($p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288$), outperforming a call-count-matched self-refinement baseline by $+0.51$ MQM ($p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288$). Severe per-verse failures (MQM$<80$) fall from $9.0\%$ to $7.6\%$, at roughly $9\times$ the per-verse inference cost of the baseline. Additionally, $J_{\text{route}}$ scores its own family's outputs $2$-$7$ MQM higher than $J_{\text{report}}$ on every one of the 12 conditions, empirically motivating the two-judge split; and a preflight screen of a 192,151-entry retrieval index against all 12 evaluation works verifies 0 reference leaks across 269 runtime checks. These are small gains on a metric saturating near 85-86.

items.title: Benchmarking Multilingual Document Understanding in Vision-Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Benchmarking Multilingual Document Understanding in Vision-Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14758v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) perform strongly on multimodal tasks, Document Understanding (DU) among them, but the benchmarks that measure them mostly cover English documents and narrow problems. How well current VLMs generalize across languages, tasks, styles and layouts therefore remains unclear. We introduce MDU, a multilingual DU benchmark of 23146 examples spanning 13 tasks and five languages: English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish. The tasks isolate complementary capabilities, from surface-level text and Markdown extraction through summarization, classification and named-entity recognition to layout-sensitive passage and layout extraction. We evaluate 45 state-of-the-art open-weight VLMs from 1.7B to 235B parameters, plus one commercial system under the same protocol. The benchmark is far from saturated: the best average is 69.0, only eight of the 45 evaluated systems reach 65, and the two best results come from 27B models rather than from the largest systems we evaluate. Performance is uneven in ways that scale does not fix. The gap between the strongest and weakest language does not close as models grow, and it survives controlling for the domain composition of each language. Capabilities also do not improve together: once we partial out overall model quality, per-task scores are largely uncorrelated, and transcription ability in particular trades off against semantic extraction.

items.title: What Do Tokenizer Comparisons Measure? Disentangling Granularity, Root Assignment, and Word-Level Readout across Amharic and Hausa [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Do Tokenizer Comparisons Measure? Disentangling Granularity, Root Assignment, and Word-Level Readout across Amharic and Hausa
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Morphology-aware tokenizers are expected to help morphologically rich languages, and their reported gains over byte-pair encoding (BPE) are usually credited to their linguistic units. A comparison with BPE cannot support this attribution, since such a tokenizer also segments text more finely (granularity) and, on token-level tasks, changes how much the sub-token readout matters. We separate both factors from the effect of grouping words by their roots (root assignment) in Amharic, a Semitic language whose Ge'ez abugida hides consonantal roots inside syllabic glyphs, with Latin-script Hausa as an orthographic contrast. Our design combines a lossless root-and-pattern tokenizer with controls that change one factor at a time, in two independent implementations. In both, real root assignment improves Amharic named-entity recognition over scrambled roots (+4.9 and +4.7 F1), and root-frequency structure explains little of this gain. In small from-scratch models, the readout choice moves F1 by up to 13.4 points and reverses the sign of every comparison of the root-and-pattern arms with BPE, whereas in two pretrained encoders it moves F1 by less than one point. The granularity effect changes sign across languages and implementations. We recommend decomposing tokenizer effects, and reporting the readout, before a gain is attributed to linguistic structure.

items.title: Do Large Language Models Show Racial and Sex Bias in Pain Management? A Counterfactual Audit of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Do Large Language Models Show Racial and Sex Bias in Pain Management? A Counterfactual Audit of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Racial and ethnic minority patients receive less pain treatment than non-Hispanic White patients, and large language models (LLMs) used as medical AI could reproduce that bias. Prior audits tested a few proprietary models, stated race explicitly and rarely measured the models' own response instability. In exploratory, non-preregistered analyses, Study 1 had four open-weight LLMs assess six acute-pain vignettes in every combination of four races and two sexes, with identity stated or cued only by a name (two names per group), comparing each identity with a White male reference on the same case and sampling seed. In Study 2, 24 configurations of 17 models, including OpenAI's GPT-4.1 mini and gpt-oss, Anthropic's Claude Haiku 4.5, Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash, Meta's Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen, with reasoning on and off and at two precisions, answered the same vignettes and the 50 clinician-written Q-Pain cases. In this single-prompt, JSON-constrained task, no difference survived correction in Study 1, none of 1,386 comparisons survived the false discovery rate in Study 2, and every pain-severity difference was equivalent to zero within one point on a 0-10 scale (within a quarter point for 237 of 238 Q-Pain comparisons). Opioid decisions were bounded less precisely (Study 1 could not exclude differences of about 20 percentage points), so they show no detected difference, not proof of none. The few differences surviving correction within a model favoured Black patients. Models differed far more from one another and across their own settings than between patients (the reference patient received the high opioid dose in 6% to 93% of responses), although serving software, provider and prompt format also differed. Fairness audits of clinical AI should use several names per group, pair comparisons on the seed, report the noise floor and test each deployed configuration.

In Study 2, 24 configurations of 17 models, including OpenAI's GPT-4.1 mini and gpt-oss, Anthropic's Claude Haiku 4.5, Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash, Meta's Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen, with reasoning on and off and at two precisions, answered the same vignettes and the 50 clinician-written Q-Pain cases. In this single-prompt, JSON-constrained task, no difference survived correction in Study 1, none of 1,386 comparisons survived the false discovery rate in Study 2, and every pain-severity difference was equivalent to zero within one point on a 0-10 scale (within a quarter point for 237 of 238 Q-Pain comparisons). Opioid decisions were bounded less precisely (Study 1 could not exclude differences of about 20 percentage points), so they show no detected difference, not proof of none. The few differences surviving correction within a model favoured Black patients. Models differed far more from one another and across their own settings than between patients (the reference patient received the high opioid dose in 6% to 93% of responses), although serving software, provider and prompt format also differed. Fairness audits of clinical AI should use several names per group, pair comparisons on the seed, report the noise floor and test each deployed configuration.

items.title: Breaking Bad: "Going Badly" Activations Drive Reward Hacking [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Breaking Bad: "Going Badly" Activations Drive Reward Hacking
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14996v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Humans often cheat when a task is going badly and a goal feels out of reach. We explore and validate an analogous idea in language models: they exhibit a similar internal pressure state that precedes reward hacking. Using everyday stories (crucially, without any hacking examples), we extract a task badness direction that rises as failures accumulate across three models we study (Qwen3.6-27B, GPT-OSS-20B, and Gemma-4-31B). On impossible or difficult coding tasks, task badness rises over the turns leading up to a hack. Further, subtracting the direction a moderate amount reduces cheating in Qwen, more than steering against desperation or task impossibility. Subtracting task badness by an even larger amount blinds the agent to its own failures, causing it to interpret failing tests as passing. However, the relationship to hacking differs across models: in GPT-OSS, the state separates hacking runs from honest solves but not honest failures. Our results suggest monitoring and mitigation strategies based on tracking this state of task badness. Further, as agents are set on more difficult and long-horizon tasks, states like this may push them toward illegible and obscured chain-of-thought, so oversight will be needed on internal representations such as this.

items.title: A Time-Frequency-Condition Multimodal Fusion Foundation Model for Universal Rotating-Machinery Fault Diagnosis under Multi-Element Heterogeneous Scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Time-Frequency-Condition Multimodal Fusion Foundation Model for Universal Rotating-Machinery Fault Diagnosis under Multi-Element Heterogeneous Scenarios
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intelligent fault diagnosis models are typically developed for a single machine under a specific set of operating conditions, such that each new machine or condition requires retraining from scratch. This one-machine-one-model paradigm scales poorly. Although transfer learning and domain generalization can reduce the labeling burden, they primarily seek domain-invariant commonality, potentially discarding machine-specific characteristics that are critical for diagnosis. This paper proposes TFC-MMFD, a time-frequency-condition multimodal fusion foundation model for rotating-machinery fault diagnosis under multi-element heterogeneous scenarios. Statistical indicators, time-frequency images, vibration sequences, and textual machine and condition descriptions are tokenized into a unified language-like space, allowing inputs of different physical origin to be represented as a single sequence. A LLaMA backbone, together with cross-modal bidirectional attention and a Q-Former, then distills this sequence into fault-mode queries. Diagnosis is performed by matching these queries against natural-language fault-mode anchors rather than fixed class indices, while regression-adversarial condition disentanglement and condition-conditioned masked pre-training improve robustness to changing conditions. Across four progressive tasks on ten public bearing datasets spanning diverse bearing types, speeds, and loads, TFC-MMFD attains 99.40% accuracy and 99.16% macro-F1, maintains over 80% accuracy on most interpolated unseen conditions without adaptation, and improves from 20.26% to 95.63% accuracy on an unseen machine with only five labeled samples per class. It outperforms the strongest of eight domain-generalization baselines by 10.57 percentage points and compares favorably with a recent bearing foundation model while using less than half of its fine-tuning data.

items.title: What Does Each Part of Speech Need? Contexts, Subspaces and Dimensions in Static Word Embeddings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Does Each Part of Speech Need? Contexts, Subspaces and Dimensions in Static Word Embeddings
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Static word embeddings give a word one vector, ignoring its different functions as noun, verb or adjective. Training on part-of-speech-tagged text gives each function its own vector, at the cost of a larger table. Using nine controlled corpora, we ask which context words each part of speech needs, whether it needs its own subspace, and whether the number of dimensions a word keeps should follow its part of speech or its frequency. The tags raise verb similarity on SimVerb-3500 at every dimension from 50 to 300 but help nouns much less. Added to verb-only text, adverbs help verbs more than as many random words; adjectives help nouns only slightly. At a fixed dimension, per-part-of-speech PCA bases preserve verb and adjective similarity better than a global basis or frequency-band bases. Nouns need more dimensions than verbs only among frequent words. We therefore allocate dimensions by frequency with these bases: at a third of the original size, only rare words lose dimensions, SimVerb-3500 and SimLex-999 nouns match the uncompressed table, and verb-to-noun retrieval stays within 0.02. Part of speech decides what a word's vector should be; frequency decides how much of it to keep.

items.title: SimRec: Learning to Search, Ask, and Recommend from Simulated Interaction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SimRec: Learning to Search, Ask, and Recommend from Simulated Interaction
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based recommendation agents can search catalogs, inspect products, ask users, and revise rejected recommendations. However, these behaviors are often governed by hand-designed workflows, while existing training methods optimize isolated components such as query rewriting or list ranking rather than the interaction policy as a whole. We present SimRec, a reinforcement learning framework that trains the full interaction policy of a tool-integrated recommendation agent. SimRec introduces two components. A task-anchored user simulator provides feedback on every recommendation: conditioned on the current task need rather than on user profile, and it can be an external LLM or the recommender itself under self-play. A task-aligned reward optimizes the whole trajectory with GRPO, crediting natural retrieval quality and valid tool use alongside the final hit, with training-only target injection to handle sparse hits over large catalogs. On ESCI and Amazon C4, SimRec improves the NDCG@100 of a Qwen3-4B agent from 32.23% to 35.42% and from 22.94% to 24.72%}, outperforming training-free agents on far larger backbones and task-aligned baselines on NDCG. Analysis shows that the trained agent verifies candidates, uses preferences, and recovers from rejected recommendations far more often than its untrained counterpart. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/SimRec .

items.title: Faithful in Steps: Improving Generalization and Citation in RAG via Query Decomposition [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Faithful in Steps: Improving Generalization and Citation in RAG via Query Decomposition
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augment generation is a prevalent strategy to mitigate hallucinations of LLMs. The attributable RAG (RAGQ) generates quotes for its answers. The quotes indicate which input contexts support the RAG to derive the answers, enhancing the answer's verifiability and trustworthiness. However, existing RAGQs exhibit significant degradation when dealing with questions that require multi-hop reasoning and multi-modal understanding, suffering from over-citation, implicit entity identification failure, and poor generalization. In this paper, we propose a novel RAGQ framework, namely QDRAG. QDRAG breaks down the input question into atomic subquestions to identify the implicit entities. Then, the reranker prunes context distractors to eliminate the downstream over-citation. To facilitate query decomposition, we propose two zero-shot approaches: QD-C and QD-R, which guide the QD MLLM to decompose the question based on context knowledge and retrieval rewards, respectively. One interesting finding is that finetuning on the QD task shows better generalizability compared to directly finetuning on the downstream RAGQ task. Experiments on four multi-modal QA benchmarks demonstrate QDRAG's efficacy in grounding answers and generating faithful citations. The framework significantly outperforms all the baselines on both in-domain and out-of-domain tests, even surpassing Gemini-Pro.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.15538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augment generation is a prevalent strategy to mitigate hallucinations of LLMs. The attributable RAG (RAGQ) generates quotes for its answers. The quotes indicate which input contexts support the RAG to derive the answers, enhancing the answer's verifiability and trustworthiness. However, existing RAGQs exhibit significant degradation when dealing with questions that require multi-hop reasoning and multi-modal understanding, suffering from over-citation, implicit entity identification failure, and poor generalization. In this paper, we propose a novel RAGQ framework, namely QDRAG. QDRAG breaks down the input question into atomic subquestions to identify the implicit entities. Then, the reranker prunes context distractors to eliminate the downstream over-citation. To facilitate query decomposition, we propose two zero-shot approaches: QD-C and QD-R, which guide the QD MLLM to decompose the question based on context knowledge and retrieval rewards, respectively. One interesting finding is that finetuning on the QD task shows better generalizability compared to directly finetuning on the downstream RAGQ task. Experiments on four multi-modal QA benchmarks demonstrate QDRAG's efficacy in grounding answers and generating faithful citations. The framework significantly outperforms all the baselines on both in-domain and out-of-domain tests, even surpassing Gemini-Pro.

items.title: Outside the Purview of the Reward: Capability Drift in Multilingual Post-Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Outside the Purview of the Reward: Capability Drift in Multilingual Post-Training
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15717v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training can improve rewarded behavior while weakening capabilities users still need. We study two GRPO branches from a shared supervised checkpoint in a multilingual mixture-of-experts model. The released branch gains 36.07 points on MATH but loses 19.32 F1 points on XQuAD-Indic, while XQuAD-English improves under the same scoring rule. An independently trained sibling adds Indic instruction following and language-aware shaping. It recovers the regressing Indic task scores and preserves MATH, but does not restore script compliance and trades off competition mathematics and code. In a later round, judge training is followed by a sharp extraction decline from the Indic branch; reward-free distillation from its earlier checkpoint restores most of the lost F1. A MATH score decomposition associates most of the measured gain with increased boxed-answer emission; accuracy among boxed answers changes little. These results show why benchmark scores should be read alongside the response forms they reward.

items.title: HeriKGQA: Grounded Knowledge-Graph Question Answering over Cultural Heritage Sensor Data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: HeriKGQA: Grounded Knowledge-Graph Question Answering over Cultural Heritage Sensor Data
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cultural heritage sites are increasingly monitored by sensor networks, but querying their data requires database expertise. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a natural-language interface, yet over raw sensor records they lose track of which sensor, site, and time each value belongs to, and silently miscompute. We present HeriKGQA, a knowledge-graph question-answering method that confines the LLM to interpreting questions and phrasing answers, leaving computation to SPARQL and deterministic code. Questions are parsed into intents constrained by a heritage ontology aligning W3C SOSA/SSN with CIDOC-CRM, compiled into SPARQL, and answered from query results and temporal, spatial, and anomaly facts derived by a grounding layer, with error correction guarding each LLM step. On 500 questions over real data from five heritage sites, HeriKGQA reaches 99.0% accuracy, 18.2 points above the strongest of three baselines using the same LLM and receiving the same anomaly rules and answer conventions, with comparable answer quality while running almost four times faster. Without grounding, accuracy drops by 12.2 points and on anomaly questions from 99% to 66%. We report lessons from development and live deployment.

items.title: ShadowBench: Exposing Lexical Anchoring and the Illusion of Forgetting in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ShadowBench: Exposing Lexical Anchoring and the Illusion of Forgetting in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as primary interfaces for factual retrieval, yet current evaluation paradigms rely almost exclusively on explicit entity names. In this work, we demonstrate that LLM knowledge is fundamentally lexically anchored: models possess extensive factual information but find it significantly difficult to retrieve without explicit name tokens. To quantify this limitation, we introduce ShadowBench, a rigorously hardened, shortcut-resistant benchmark designed to evaluate Latent Entity Association via a novel Dual-Trait Association (DTA) task. Our evaluation reveals a pervasive "Shadow Gap" across all model scales$\unicode{x2013}$up to the frontier models GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4.6$\unicode{x2013}$where removing lexical anchors causes performance drops of over 20%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this lexical dependency exposes a critical vulnerability in AI safety. Applying ShadowBench to Machine Unlearning, we find that state-of-the-art algorithms (e.g., Gradient Difference, NPO) achieve only superficial lexical erasure. While unlearned models fail on direct queries, our novel Latent Entity Leakage Rate (LELR) metric reveals that for popular entities, models explicitly reconstruct the "forgotten" entity in their internal reasoning traces in over 74% of cases, utilizing residual shadow knowledge to solve associative tasks. Conversely, for niche entities, models retain high shadow accuracy (60-90%) via implicit attribute correlation despite 0% LELR. Ultimately, ShadowBench indicates that current unlearning paradigms create an "Illusion of Forgetting," demonstrating that existing methods act as superficial output filters and are not yet reliable for achieving true parametric erasure.

items.title: Show Your Work in Swahili: Reinforcement Learning for Native-Language Mathematical Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Show Your Work in Swahili: Reinforcement Learning for Native-Language Mathematical Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16104v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Fikiria, a two-stage SFT+GRPO recipe for Swahili mathematical reasoning. Its reward multiplies a format gate by a weighted sum of answer accuracy and the ChrF\texttt{++} similarity of the Swahili reasoning to an in-language reference chain of thought, so that training targets the surface fidelity of the reasoning trace and not only the final answer. We train on a 2.3k-problem Swahili dataset created by translating GSM8K with GPT-4.1 and filtering with SSA-COMET. On AfriMGSM Swahili, Fikiria-AfriqueQwen-14B reaches 79.2\%. Under the same fixed prompt and strict answer-format scoring, GPT-4o reaches 68.0\%, partly because it often fails the required answer format; IrokoBench reports 78.8\% for GPT-4o using a best-per-model prompt, a figure numerically close to ours but not directly comparable. In a small human evaluation with co-author annotators, GPT-4o's outputs were preferred overall. ChrF\texttt{++} measures surface fidelity, not the validity of individual reasoning steps.

items.title: Temporal Context-Aware Spam Detection Using Transformer-Based NLP Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Temporal Context-Aware Spam Detection Using Transformer-Based NLP Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spam detection is usually treated as single-message classification, ignoring behavioral patterns that emerge across sequences of messages from the same sender. We study outbound SMS spam detection at the carrier level, where the goal is to predict at send time whether a carrier will flag a message as spam. Using a proprietary production database of 43,741 outbound SMS messages with UTC transmission timestamps and carrier delivery statuses, we report three sets of results. On an 8,749-message held-out test set, a TF-IDF + logistic regression baseline reaches AUC-ROC 0.8721, and a text-only DeBERTa-v3-base classifier reaches AUC-ROC 0.9011 and F1 0.8412. A deployed DistilBERT model augmented with inter-message temporal features reaches accuracy 0.8238, spam-class F1 0.8382, and recall 0.9128 at threshold 0.5 on a separate, class-balanced 20,000-message production evaluation set; these results are not directly comparable with the held-out test results. We also describe TemporalBertSpam, an architecture that encodes each sender's message history with a causal Transformer, and outline the same-split evaluation needed to measure its contribution.

items.title: Data-Efficient LLM Safety Alignment Guided by Interpretable Features [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Data-Efficient LLM Safety Alignment Guided by Interpretable Features
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16183v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing large language models typically rely on massive fine-tuning datasets for safety alignment, which results in higher costs for safety alignment and often leads to the problem of over-refusal. We propose Less is Safer (LIS), a compact yet highly effective dataset for safety alignment, constructed through interpretable feature-guided selection and adversarial synthesis. Specifically, we leverage Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) activations to efficiently select prompts that cover diverse and interpretable safety features. Then, we employ a multi-agent adversarial synthesis framework to generate harmless prompts that nevertheless elicit unnecessary refusals. LIS contains only 2.4K samples, yet outperforms much larger datasets, e.g., TRIDENT-Core (26K), TRIDENT-Edge (19K) and WildJailbreak (262K), in overall performance on four safety and five over-refusal benchmarks. Through ablation experiments, we demonstrate that neither safety data nor over-refusal data alone can achieve optimal results. We also used safety features from SAE, annotated by an LLM, for data filtering, but the results were inferior to those obtained using the pipeline proposed in this paper.

items.title: Indic-Task Gains and Regressions after Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Indic-Task Gains and Regressions after Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We run reinforcement learning (RL) with GRPO across four environments, starting from a supervised fine-tuned 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model covering English and eight Indic languages. We compare the model before and after RL across 34 benchmarks in one evaluation campaign. MATH improves by 36.07 points, and most Indic benchmarks also improve. Yet XQuAD-Indic F1 falls 19.32 points as English answers rise from 8.7% to 91.7%; IndicQA falls 8.64, while English XQuAD gains 11.71 F1. A second RL run from the same supervised initialization adds an Indic environment together with language and repetition rewards. Compared with the released model, it improves both passage-answering and instruction-following benchmarks, along with preserving MATH performance. But it loses ground on reasoning and coding benchmarks. Several training choices changed together, so we cannot isolate the effect of any one of the reward terms. Script compliance remains unresolved. Adding a language reward did not ensure use of the requested script. Passage answering and script compliance therefore need direct evaluation, even when other benchmark scores improve.

items.title: Label-Efficient Document-Grounded Factuality Detection via Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Label-Efficient Document-Grounded Factuality Detection via Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent claims that are unsupported by a given source document, motivating accurate and efficient document-grounded factuality detection. Existing LLM-based evaluators often require repeated inference and incur high computational cost, whereas compact factuality detectors are efficient at inference time but commonly rely on large labeled or synthetically generated corpora. We propose CPIL (Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning), a two-stage Siamese framework that converts a small labeled set into relational supervision without acquiring additional factuality labels. CPIL constructs positive pairs from distinct label-preserving paraphrastic views of the same document-claim instance and negative pairs from opposite-label examples associated with the same source document. It further introduces quantile-aware semi-hard negative mining, which derives a boundary from the positive-pair similarity distribution and balances informative negatives with broader coverage. In the two-stage training procedure, Stage 1 learns an encoder from these task-aware pairs, and Stage 2 jointly fine-tunes the encoder and a linear classification head for binary factuality prediction. At inference time, CPIL requires no paraphrase generation, pair construction, or Siamese comparison and uses only one encoder-classifier forward pass. On the 11-task LLM-AggreFact benchmark, CPIL-2% and CPIL-3% achieve macro-F1 scores of 81.04 and 81.60 while using only 2-3% of the FactCG-released labeled pool. Both settings outperform all compared compact detectors and two vanilla LLM references. Ablations and sensitivity analyses support the contributions of task-aware pair construction, dynamic negative mining, and multi-pivot paraphrasing.

items.title: Beyond Compressing Everything: Contrastive Memory Learning for Selective Context Compression [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Compressing Everything: Contrastive Memory Learning for Selective Context Compression
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16384v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance toward increasingly long inputs, soft context compression offers a promising approach to efficient inference by converting long inputs into compact memory slots. Under limited memory budgets, effective context compression remains challenging because task-relevant evidence varies substantially across queries, ranging from localized evidence to multiple distant spans or information dispersed throughout the full document. Instead of compressing everything indiscriminately, we propose CoMem, a query-guided selective context compression framework that learns memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query. CoMem develops Contrastive Compressor Learning to achieve query-sensitive yet context-preserving memory representations. To inject a strong prior over query-dependent evidence distributions, we devise a same-context hard negative mining strategy by pairing a single document with multiple queries, requiring the compressor to selectively retain information according to each query's distinct evidence needs. To address the restricted information flow imposed by causal masking, we further enable bidirectional attention among memory slots. Experiments demonstrate that CoMem consistently outperforms existing context compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/scar-on/CoMem.

items.title: Where in the Input Does a One-Pass Decision Encoder Look? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Where in the Input Does a One-Pass Decision Encoder Look?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Laya is a small model that answers a multiple-choice question about a text in one pass: the question, the options (each with a name and a description) and the text form one sequence of at most 512 tokens, the window, in the English release. A longer text is silently cut at the end, and we measure what that costs. Test documents place a held-out row's text, the evidence, at a chosen token offset among distractor text; 177 items, five tasks, three checkpoints (released, short-row fine-tune, long-document fine-tune), four window sizes and 93,275 scored requests. When the evidence lies beyond the window, accuracy falls to 26.4% for the released checkpoint (27.2% for both fine-tunes), near the 27.0% of guessing and below the 35.6% of always giving the commonest label. Confidence gives no warning (AUROC 0.50 to 0.55 for telling cut from read requests; 0.5 = chance), and the runtime's truncation flag also fires on requests whose evidence was visible. The released checkpoint reads visible evidence badly once text precedes it: 38.5% pooled against 60% when the evidence comes first, so a larger window alone gains +6.2 points. Fine-tuning on long documents adds +27.6 points on visible evidence over the short-row fine-tune (95% interval +22.3 to +33.1) and nothing on cut evidence. That is an in-family result: training rows and test documents share generator and question types, and the main filler is of the training kind. With encyclopedic filler never seen in training the gain is +13.2 (+9.9 to +16.6), with rows of other tasks as filler -2.0. Among training-free rearrangements a 312-token window scan helps most (+11.9 points over the default for the released checkpoint) at six to eleven forward passes. Documents are synthetic, labels are LLM-made and one backbone is studied, so these diagnose this model, not long documents in general.

items.originalTitle: MuSeToM: Multi-Sensory Evaluation of Belief Revision with Textual Cues Across Six Senses
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM), the ability to infer mental states in others, is pivotal for human social cognition. Existing evaluations of ToM in large language models (LLMs) mainly focus on static belief attribution and false-belief reasoning, leaving a critical aspect of social reasoning underexplored: can LLMs decide whether perceptual evidence is sufficient to justify another person's belief revision? To address this gap, we present MuSeToM, a human-validated, text-based benchmark for evaluating epistemic belief revision in ToM reasoning. MuSeToM contains 2,415 instances adapted from BigToM and OpenToM, with textual cues spanning six sensory categories, and tests whether models can determine when a protagonist should revise a belief and infer the resulting updated belief state. Using MuSeToM, we systematically evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs under direct and chain-of-thought prompting, revealing a pronounced dissonance: while models often detect that a belief may change, they struggle to identify the updated belief and frequently over-update on perceptually salient but epistemically insufficient cues.

items.title: Pretraining Data Statistics Shape the Phases of Learning Entity Comparison in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Pretraining Data Statistics Shape the Phases of Learning Entity Comparison in Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16882v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How does data shape language model (LM) behavior throughout pretraining? We investigate this question through a case study on entity comparison, e.g., Between France and Brazil, which country is larger?, across nine comparison tasks spanning five entity types. We begin with controlled experiments in which we train small LMs (163M parameters) on mixtures of natural text from pretraining corpora and synthetic task data. Our analysis identifies three distinct phases of learning: (1) an early phase where the LM selects entities by frequency, (2) a middle phase where the LM selects entities by position in the prompt (first vs. last mentioned entity), and (3) a late phase where the LM selects the entity that is the correct answer. We show that the emergence of these three phases is causally determined by statistical properties of the training data. With small amounts of task-specific synthetic data, we observe only the first two phases and the model fails to learn the task; with large amounts, the model jumps directly from the frequency-based heuristic to solving the task correctly. Moreover, changing the entity frequency distribution from a naturally occurring Zipfian distribution (a small number of entities are very common and the vast majority are rare) to a uniform one weakens the frequency phase and speeds up learning of the task. Lastly, we show that the three phases of training dynamics from our controlled experiments appear in the open source model OLMo-2 32B. Together, our findings demonstrate that properties of pretraining data are causal drivers of heuristic learning and show that small-scale synthetic experiments can predict training dynamics at larger scales.
